evidence_source: Froguel P et al. Close linkage of glucokinase locus on chromosome 7p to early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Nature 1992;356:162-164; Vionnet N et al. Nonsense mutation in the glucokinase gene causes early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Nature 1992;356:721-722
stop_reason: not stopped
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT02561338 (Hua Medicine) was a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 12-week Phase 2 trial of HMS5552 (dorzagliatin) in 258 adults with T2D, started September 2015. HbA1c fell in a dose-dependent way (-0.39% to -1.12% vs -0.35% for placebo). Earlier industry trials of this entity were Phase 1 only.

The program advanced within 4 years. Hua Medicine started two Phase 3 trials in 2017: SEED (NCT03173391, started 2017-07-18) and DAWN (NCT03141073, started 2017-10-15). Both met their 24-week HbA1c primary endpoints (SEED: -1.07% vs -0.50%; DAWN: -1.02% vs -0.36%; published in Nature Medicine 2022). China's NMPA approved dorzagliatin for T2D in September 2022. There is no FDA approval, and a post-marketing Phase 4 safety study (NCT06263348) followed. If the benchmark requires approval specifically by the FDA, the Phase 3 start still meets the 'advanced' criterion.

evidence.earliest_source: Froguel P et al. Close linkage of glucokinase locus on chromosome 7p to early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Nature 1992;356:162-164; Vionnet N et al. Nonsense mutation in the glucokinase gene causes early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Nature 1992;356:721-722
evidence.notes: 1. Dorzagliatin (HMS5552, Hua Medicine) is an allosteric glucokinase activator; target GCK and 'increases function' are correct. 2. Type 2 diabetes (MONDO:0005148) is the indication studied in the Phase 2 programme; mapping is sound. 3. Heterozygous loss-of-function GCK mutations cause MODY2 (GCK-MODY, OMIM 125851), and homozygous/compound heterozygous loss of function causes permanent neonatal diabetes (OMIM 606176); activating mutations cause hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia. MODY was originally described as early-onset non-insulin-dependent diabetes, so it counts as a closely related subtype of T2D. ClinVar lists many pathogenic GCK variants for MODY2. Common GCK promoter variants also associate with fasting glucose and T2D in GWAS. 4. The 1992 linkage and mutation reports long predate the 2015 Phase 2 entry, and the direction (loss of function causes diabetes; the drug raises function) is consistent. 5. Not authored by Hua Medicine. No data errors found.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349(6311):704-6 (PMID 1671712). It reports APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar RCV000019714 / VCV 18088, NM_000484.4(APP):c.2149G>A, Pathogenic for Alzheimer disease type 1.
outcome_summary:
The industry-sponsored Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04693520 is an open-label biomarker study by Alzheon of ALZ-801 in APOE4 carriers with early Alzheimer's disease. It started on 2020-09-30 (actual), and ClinicalTrials.gov lists it as COMPLETED.

The program advanced within four years. Alzheon's Phase 3 APOLLOE4 trial (NCT04770220; 325 APOE4/4 patients with early Alzheimer's disease; 265 mg twice daily vs placebo for 78 weeks) started on 2021-05-19 and completed in 2024.

APOLLOE4 missed its primary endpoint, ADAS-Cog13 (the cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale). The posted results give a least-squares mean difference of -0.51 with p=0.6058. Alzheon's topline release of 2025-04-10 says the primary endpoint was 'not met' (11% slowing, p=0.607). The key secondary clinical outcomes also showed no effect in the overall population. Hippocampal atrophy slowed significantly (18%, p=0.017). In the prespecified MCI subgroup (MMSE above 26, N=125) results were only nominally significant: ADAS-Cog13 p=0.041, DAD p=0.016, CDR-SB p=0.053. The full results were published in Drugs in 2025. The common adverse events were gastrointestinal, and there was no increase in ARIA (the brain swelling and bleeding seen with amyloid antibodies). Plasma p-tau217 fell significantly in the overall population (Drugs, 2026).

The Phase 3 long-term extension (NCT06304883) was TERMINATED in March 2026, with the reason given as 'Sponsor business decision'.

Current status: the drug is not approved and no marketing application has been filed. As of October 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists no new Phase 3 trial. Alzheon's press releases still describe the drug as 'currently in Phase 3 development' (April 2026). In February and September 2026 the company said it is 'moving forward with plans for the next Phase 3 study', which appears to focus on APOE4/4 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The program has not been formally stopped.

On the coding: because the program advanced to Phase 3 within the window, the failure code is not_a_failure. However, the advancing Phase 3 itself failed its primary endpoint. If that trial were coded as a failure, the best code would be F3 (wrong disease stage, with benefit limited to MCI). status_now is a judgment call: the program is in Phase 3 by the company's own description, but no Phase 3 trial is active and nothing has been filed.

evidence.earliest_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349(6311):704-6 (PMID 1671712). It reports APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar RCV000019714 / VCV 18088, NM_000484.4(APP):c.2149G>A, Pathogenic for Alzheimer disease type 1.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: valiltramiprosate (ALZ-801) is an oral valine prodrug of tramiprosate. ChEMBL lists both valiltramiprosate (CHEMBL4650301) and tramiprosate (CHEMBL149082) as an 'Amyloid-beta A4 protein stabiliser', action type STABILISER, on target CHEMBL2487 (amyloid-beta precursor protein, APP). The drug acts on the Abeta42 peptide, a cleavage product of APP: it binds Abeta42 monomers, stabilises them and inhibits oligomer formation (Kocis 2017 CNS Drugs; Hey 2018 Clin Pharmacokinet). This is not inhibition or activation of APP itself, so the recorded 'APP (other)' fits. Both mechanism papers are from Alzheon. Neurochem's independent Gervais 2007 Neurobiol Aging paper describes tramiprosate keeping soluble Abeta non-fibrillar.

(2) Entry trial: NCT04693520 (Alzheon, Phase 2, single arm, ALZ-801 265 mg BID) studied 'Early Alzheimer's Disease' in APOE4/4 and APOE3/4 carriers. Its actual start date is 2020-09-30, which matches phase2_entry. Mapping to MONDO:0004975 is correct.

(3) Claim: true. The ClinVar records in the evidence rows check out. RCV000019714 = V717I (London), RCV000019715 = V717F (Indiana), RCV000019716 = V717G, RCV000019718 = A692G (Flemish), RCV000019725 = E693G (Arctic). All are germline Pathogenic in ClinVar. In MONDO, Alzheimer disease type 1 (MONDO:0007088) is a descendant of Alzheimer disease (MONDO:0004975), through early-onset autosomal dominant AD and familial AD. The earliest primary paper is Goate et al., Nature, February 1991, which describes V717I segregating with familial AD. Other 1991 papers confirm it: Naruse and van Duijn in Lancet (April 1991), Yoshioka in BBRC, and Murrell in Science (October 1991, V717F). All of these are about 29 years before the September 2020 Phase 2 entry.

Caveats: the APP evidence covers rare autosomal dominant early-onset AD (AD1). The trial enrolled APOE4 carriers with early, mostly sporadic AD, so the link is to a subtype, not to the trial's exact population. The evidence row dating E693G (RCV000019725) to 1992 is questionable: the Arctic mutation is usually credited to a 2001 paper, and the 1992 date seems to come from a 1992 AJHG citation in ClinVar (Kamino et al., PMID 1415269). This does not affect the conclusion. The 1990 genomics_england row has no traceable paper and was not used.

(4) Sponsor: the Goate paper comes from St Mary's Hospital Medical School, London, and has no connection to Alzheon. Only the mechanism papers are sponsor-authored, not the genetic evidence.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Kadowaki T et al., 'Two mutant alleles of the insulin receptor gene in a patient with extreme insulin resistance', Science 1988 (PMID 2834824) - INSR loss-of-function causes Mendelian insulin-resistant diabetes (type A insulin resistance / Donohue / Rabson-Mendenhall, OMIM 147670). Direct T2D link: Cocozza S et al., Diabetes 1992 (PMID 1607076), INSR R1152Q (R1191Q) in an NIDDM patient, ClinVar SCV000036082 (OMIM 147670.0021) Pathogenic for type 2 diabetes mellitus.
stop_reason: n/a (approved)
outcome_summary:
The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of LY3209590 (insulin efsitora alfa) in type 2 diabetes is Eli Lilly's NCT03736785, a randomized open-label trial vs degludec in insulin-treated T2D (n=399), with an actual start of 2018-11-15, matching the pipeline date. Earlier LY3209590 trials (NCT02942914, NCT03367377, NCT03603704) were Phase 1; a second T2D Phase 2 (NCT04450394) started 2020-07-01.

The program advanced within 4 years: the Phase 3 QWINT program began with NCT05275400 (QWINT-3, T2D, start 2022-03-08), followed by QWINT-2 (NCT05362058, start 2022-06-03), QWINT-4 (NCT05462756, 2022-08-11) and QWINT-1 (NCT05662332, 2023-01-14), all completed with results posted, each with an HbA1c noninferiority primary endpoint. Per Lilly and trade press, efsitora met noninferior HbA1c reduction versus daily glargine or degludec across the four T2D trials.

The FDA approved insulin efsitora alfa-gobe (Onswik) on 2026-09-24 for adults with type 2 diabetes, after approvals in the EU, Mexico and Japan (Lilly press release; Medscape; HCPLive).

evidence.earliest_source: Kadowaki T et al., 'Two mutant alleles of the insulin receptor gene in a patient with extreme insulin resistance', Science 1988 (PMID 2834824) - INSR loss-of-function causes Mendelian insulin-resistant diabetes (type A insulin resistance / Donohue / Rabson-Mendenhall, OMIM 147670). Direct T2D link: Cocozza S et al., Diabetes 1992 (PMID 1607076), INSR R1152Q (R1191Q) in an NIDDM patient, ClinVar SCV000036082 (OMIM 147670.0021) Pathogenic for type 2 diabetes mellitus.
evidence.notes:
1. Efsitora alfa (LY3209590, basal insulin-Fc) is a once-weekly insulin analogue; it is an INSR agonist, so target INSR and action 'increases function' are correct.
2. MONDO:0005148 type 2 diabetes is the right mapping; the Phase 2 trial NCT03736785 (T2D patients on basal insulin) began 2018-11-15, which matches the recorded date.
3. Mendelian INSR loss-of-function syndromes (type A insulin resistance, Rabson-Mendenhall, Donohue) cause insulin-resistant diabetes, a disease very similar to T2D. Kadowaki 1988 and Yoshimasa 1988 (Science) established this.
4. ClinVar has an OMIM-curated 'Pathogenic' assertion (no assertion criteria) linking INSR R1191Q (legacy R1152Q) to type 2 diabetes mellitus (RCV000015815), based on Cocozza 1992. The evidence is weak: one patient, and Esposito 1995 (PMID 7814014) did not replicate it in 68 Italian NIDDM patients. The variant's aggregate ClinVar classification is now 'conflicting'. The claim holds on the letter of the rule, but the evidence that INSR is Mendelian for common T2D specifically is thin; the strong evidence is for the monogenic insulin-resistance syndromes.
5. None of these sources is by Eli Lilly. No data errors found.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
error_source: DATA ERROR: the action at GABRA1 should be recorded as an increase in target function (partial agonist/PAM at the benzodiazepine site), not 'ambiguous'.
evidence_source: Cossette P et al. Mutation of GABRA1 in an autosomal dominant form of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Nat Genet 2002;31:184-189 (GABRA1 A322D; OMIM 611136 EJM5; ClinVar pathogenic GABRA1 variants for epilepsy)
stop_reason: UCB terminated the padsevonil program in 2020 after the Phase 2b ARISE trial missed its primary efficacy endpoints and DUET also showed no significant benefit; insufficient benefit over existing antiseizure drugs
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: the earliest industry Phase 2 trial is UCB's EP0069 (NCT02495844, UCB0942 in highly drug-resistant focal epilepsy), actual start July 2015, n=55. Its primary endpoint (75% responder rate during the 2-week inpatient period) gave 30.8% vs 11.1% on placebo, p=0.068.

The program advanced within 4 years. The Phase 3 DUET trial (NCT03739840) started 2019-03-06, inside the 4-year window from 2015-07-01. The Phase 2b ARISE trial (NCT03373383, start 2018-02-12, n=411) missed its primary endpoint: placebo-adjusted seizure-frequency reductions were 12-19% with p=0.06-0.25 across doses (CT.gov results). UCB announced the ARISE miss in March 2020. DUET was then terminated (primary p=0.687), along with the Phase 2 open-label extension and the Phase 1 studies, all with the stated reason 'UCB has decided to stop development of padsevonil'.

Status: stopped (2020). Because the Phase 3 start counts as an advance, the failure code is not_a_failure. The later discontinuation looks like efficacy that did not translate (F2-like), not a failure to advance.

evidence.earliest_source: Cossette P et al. Mutation of GABRA1 in an autosomal dominant form of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Nat Genet 2002;31:184-189 (GABRA1 A322D; OMIM 611136 EJM5; ClinVar pathogenic GABRA1 variants for epilepsy)
evidence.notes:
1. Padsevonil binds SV2A, SV2B and SV2C with nanomolar affinity and the GABAA receptor benzodiazepine site with low-to-moderate affinity (pKi ~6.4) as a partial agonist/positive allosteric modulator (Wood et al. JPET 2020; Niespodziany et al. Epilepsia 2020). The SV2 targets are right. GABRA1 is a fair proxy, but the benzodiazepine site is formed at the alpha(1/2/3/5)-gamma2 interface, so GABRA1 alone is only part of the GABAA target.
2. 'Ambiguous' action is accurate for SV2 ligands, whose functional effect on SV2A is not defined. At the GABAA receptor the action is clearly positive modulation (increases function), so the recorded action is only partly right.
DATA ERROR: the action at GABRA1 should be recorded as an increase in target function (partial agonist/PAM at the benzodiazepine site), not 'ambiguous'.
3. Epilepsy (MONDO:0005027) is the right parent term for focal-onset drug-resistant epilepsy.
4. Mendelian evidence: GABRA1 germline mutations cause autosomal dominant juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (Cossette 2002) and later epileptic encephalopathies. ClinVar has many GABRA1 variants classed pathogenic for epilepsy. These loss-of-function variants point the same way as the drug's positive modulation.
5. SV2A: a homozygous R383Q variant was reported in intractable infantile epilepsy (Serajee & Huq, Pediatr Neurol 2015;52:642-646). That is a single family, published in 2015 close to the Phase 2 entry, so the claim rests on GABRA1.
6. Cossette et al. are an academic group (Rouleau lab, Montreal), not UCB.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Wang L et al., Gain-of-function variants in SYK cause immune dysregulation and systemic inflammation in humans and mice, Nat Genet 53:500-510 (closest Mendelian SYK evidence; not RA)
stop_reason: The global Phase 2 in active RA (inadequate response to MTX/anti-TNF) missed its primary endpoint, change in DAS28-hsCRP at week 12 (topline January 2021). Safety was clean. Oscotec said a higher dose might improve efficacy, but it has run no further RA trial and has focused cevidoplenib on immune thrombocytopenia.
outcome_summary:
The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of cevidoplenib (SKI-O-703, an oral SYK inhibitor) in RA is Oscotec's NCT04057118, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study (100/200/400 mg BID, n=163), with an actual start of 2019-03-20 (matching the pipeline date) and completion on 2020-10-13. The other cevidoplenib Phase 2, NCT04056195, is in ITP.

In January 2021 Korea Biomedical Review reported that the trial missed its primary endpoint (DAS28-hsCRP change at week 12) and showed no significant effect on remission, with no serious toxicity. Oscotec said it expected 'to improve efficacy by increasing the dose' and would consider further testing, but CT.gov lists no later RA trial; later cevidoplenib trials are ITP, ADME and bioequivalence studies, and the drug received FDA orphan designation for ITP.

Failure code F1 is a judgement call. SYK inhibition is clinically validated in RA (fostamatinib), and the sponsor attributed the miss to insufficient dose, so the likeliest explanation is inadequate exposure or engagement at the doses tested; no target-engagement data were reported. Status 'stopped' is inferred from the absence of RA activity since 2021; no formal discontinuation announcement was found.

evidence.earliest_source: Wang L et al., Gain-of-function variants in SYK cause immune dysregulation and systemic inflammation in humans and mice, Nat Genet 53:500-510 (closest Mendelian SYK evidence; not RA)
evidence.notes:
1. Cevidoplenib (SKI-O-703, Oscotec) is a selective SYK inhibitor; target SYK and action 'decreases' are correct.
2. RA mapping to MONDO:0008383 is sound.
3. The only Mendelian/ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence for SYK is monoallelic gain-of-function variants causing immunodeficiency with multi-organ inflammation (colitis, arthritis, dermatitis) and B-cell lymphoma (OMIM 600085 / Immunodeficiency 82 with systemic inflammation), published 2021. That syndrome is not RA or a very similar disease (arthritis is one feature of a systemic autoinflammatory/immunodeficiency disorder), and it postdates the 2019-03-20 Phase 2 entry.
4. No ClinVar pathogenic SYK germline variant curated for RA or an RA subtype was found; RA genetic evidence is polygenic GWAS and SYK is not an established RA Mendelian gene.
5. Claim not supported on either the disease link or the date. No data errors found in target, action, disease.

failure_second.rationale: Posted results for NCT04057118 (n=163) show the week-12 change in DAS was -0.95 on placebo against -0.91, -1.06 and -1.15 at 100, 200 and 400 mg BID: a high placebo response and only a shallow dose trend, with no significant difference. Eligibility required inadequate response to anti-TNF agents. Oscotec attributed the miss mainly to the refractory population ('many of the recruited patients had serious RA') and saw promise in less severe RA. Fostamatinib also failed its primary endpoint in TNF-inadequate responders while working in MTX-inadequate responders, so a wrong-population explanation has clinical precedent. The sponsor also mentioned a dose increase, so F1 is a plausible alternative, but no PK or engagement data were reported. Confidence is low.

adjudication.rationale: NCT04057118 (start 2019-03-20, n=163) enrolled RA patients with inadequate response to csDMARDs and anti-TNF biologics. Posted week-12 DAS28-hsCRP changes were -0.95 placebo vs -0.91/-1.06/-1.15 at 100/200/400 mg BID: no separation and only a shallow dose trend. Oscotec's stated explanation (Korea Biomedical Review, Jan 2021) was the patient population ('many of the recruited patients had serious RA'), and there is direct class precedent: fostamatinib failed in TNF-inadequate responders while showing efficacy in MTX-inadequate responders. No PK or target-engagement data were reported, so an exposure explanation (F1, the sponsor's secondary dose-increase remark) cannot be excluded, but the refractory-population explanation is better supported by the sponsor's attribution and class precedent. Confidence low-moderate.

1. Globalagliatin (SY-004, Yabao Pharmaceutical) is an allosteric glucokinase activator; target GCK and 'increases target function' are correct.
2. Type 2 diabetes mapping is sound for the indication; Phase 1 MAD in T2DM (NCT03414892) started 2018-01-03, consistent with a Phase 2 entry in Dec 2019 (Phase 2 not found on ClinicalTrials.gov, likely a Chinese registry; date not independently verified).

evidence.earliest_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349:704-6 (PMID 1671712). It describes APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar VCV000018088 / RCV000019714: Pathogenic, multiple submitters with no conflicts, Alzheimer disease type 1.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: donanemab (LY3002813) is a humanized IgG1 that binds insoluble N-truncated pyroglutamate amyloid beta (Abeta p3-42) and reduces amyloid plaques (Kisunla FDA label, sections 11 and 12.1). Abeta is a cleavage product of APP, so mapping the target to the APP gene is the usual convention. Calling it a depleter fits, because the drug clears Abeta plaque. Before Phase 2 entry, Lilly's own preclinical paper (DeMattos 2012, Neuron, PMID 23217740, Lilly authors) showed that the parent plaque-specific antibody against Abeta(p3-42), mE8, cleared existing plaque. Alzforum records donanemab as a humanized antibody derived from mE8, with Phase 1 running from May 2013 (NCT01837641, start date 2013-05-03). The label postdates entry; it is cited only to confirm the mechanism.
(2) Entry trial: NCT03367403 is TRAILBLAZER-ALZ, Phase 2, sponsored by Eli Lilly, condition 'Alzheimer Disease', in early symptomatic AD with amyloid and tau PET entry criteria. Its actual start date, 2017-12-18, matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. The evidence disease, Alzheimer disease type 1 (familial early-onset AD caused by APP), is a subtype of the trial disease.
(3) Claim: ClinVar confirms germline Pathogenic APP variants for Alzheimer disease type 1:
- VCV18088, V717I: criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts.
- VCV18089, V717F: multiple submitters, no conflicts.
- VCV18090, V717G: single submitter. Its aggregate trait now reads 'not provided', but the RCV in our row is AD type 1.
- VCV18091, A692G (Flemish): no assertion criteria.
- VCV18098, E693G (Arctic): no assertion criteria.
Primary papers:
- Goate 1991, Nature (V717I). This is the earliest.
- Murrell 1991, Science 254:97 (V717F, PMID 1925564).
- Chartier-Harlin 1991, Nature 353:844 (codon 717, PMID 1944558).
- Naruse 1991 and van Duijn 1991, both Lancet (V717I replication).
The genomics_england row dated 1990 most likely reflects Levy 1990, Science (PMID 2111584). That paper concerns an APP mutation in hereditary cerebral hemorrhage, Dutch type (cerebral amyloid angiopathy), not AD itself, so the earliest AD-specific evidence is 1991.
The genetics points the same way as the drug: the pathogenic APP mutations sit in or near the Abeta region and cause early-onset AD, and Jonsson 2012, Nature 488:96 (PMID 22801501) found a protective APP variant (A673T). Together these support lowering Abeta.
(4) All of the key sources (1991, 1992, 2012) are more than 25 years older than the 2017-12-18 entry date.
(5) Goate 1991 comes from St Mary's Hospital Medical School, London, and the other genetics papers are academic. None were written by Lilly. Only the preclinical antibody paper (DeMattos 2012) is sponsor-authored, and it is not the genetic evidence.
Clinical outcome was not researched.

outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: REAL 3 (NCT02616562) is Novo Nordisk's randomized dose-finding Phase 2 of once-weekly somapacitan vs daily Norditropin in GH-treatment-naive prepubertal children with growth hormone deficiency, actual start 2016-03-31, n=76. Caveat: earlier Novo Nordisk Phase 3 trials (REAL 1 NCT02229851, 2014; REAL 2 NCT02382939, 2015) were in adult GHD. If the MONDO term were read to include adult GHD, Phase 3 would predate this Phase 2. For childhood GHD (pituitary dwarfism), REAL 3 is the earliest Phase 2.

Advancement: the pivotal Phase 3 REAL 4 (NCT03811535, n=200) started 2019-05-20, within 4 years. It met its non-inferiority primary endpoint: 52-week height velocity was 11.2 cm/yr on somapacitan vs 11.8 cm/yr on Norditropin, difference -0.5 (95% CI -1.1 to 0.2), within the non-inferiority margin.

evidence.earliest_source: Godowski PJ et al., 'Characterization of the human growth hormone receptor gene and demonstration of a partial gene deletion in two patients with Laron-type dwarfism', PNAS 1989 (PMID 2813379); concurrently Amselem S et al., NEJM 1989 (PMID 2779634)
evidence.notes:
1. Somapacitan is a long-acting albumin-binding GH derivative; it is a GHR agonist, so target GHR and action 'increases target function' are correct.
2. MONDO:0006909 'pituitary dwarfism' is defined as growth failure due to inadequate pituitary GH production (= GH deficiency), which matches somapacitan's GHD indication.
3. Germline GHR loss-of-function causes Laron syndrome (GH insensitivity, OMIM 262500; historically 'Laron-type pituitary dwarfism'); Godowski 1989 and Amselem 1989 first showed GHR mutations. Goddard 1995 NEJM (PMID 7565946) extended heterozygous GHR mutations to idiopathic short stature (OMIM 604271).
4. MONDO places 'short stature due to partial GHR deficiency' (MONDO:0011420) as a child of MONDO:0006909, and Open Targets shows GHR-pituitary dwarfism with genetic_association score 0.83 and genetic_literature 0.83 (ClinVar/Orphanet/Gene2Phenotype-type evidence). So the claim holds as written via a MONDO subtype.
5. Caveat: the genetic link is to GH insensitivity (a receptor defect), not to GH deficiency. In that condition the pituitary output is normal and an exogenous GHR agonist cannot fix it. The direction (loss of GHR signalling gives short stature; the drug raises signalling) agrees with the drug, but the Mendelian disease is mechanistically distinct from the treated population. Placing it under 'pituitary dwarfism' is arguably an ontology artifact.
6. The sources are academic (Genentech/Stanford and INSERM) and not Novo Nordisk, the somapacitan sponsor. No data error in target, action or disease. Phase 2 date not independently contradicted.

evidence.earliest_source: Hutton M et al. Association of missense and 5'-splice-site mutations in tau with the inherited dementia FTDP-17. Nature 1998;393:702-705 (includes R406W, a mutation whose carriers are often clinically diagnosed with AD)
evidence.notes: 1. Zagotenemab (LY3303560, Eli Lilly) is a humanized antibody against aggregated/conformational tau; target MAPT is correct. 'Decreases function' is a reasonable reading of neutralizing or clearing pathological tau, though the antibody does not lower normal tau function. 2. Alzheimer disease (MONDO:0004975) is the Phase 2 indication; mapping is sound. 3. Mendelian MAPT mutations (ClinVar/OMIM pathogenic) cause frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism-17 / FTLD-tau (OMIM 600274), not Alzheimer disease, which has amyloid plus tau pathology and APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 as its Mendelian genes. Some MAPT mutations (e.g. R406W, V337M) produce an AD-like amnestic phenotype with tau filaments in the Alzheimer fold and are frequently diagnosed clinically as AD, so MAPT has Mendelian evidence for a closely related tauopathy dementia. Common-variant AD evidence at the MAPT 17q21.31 locus (e.g. Jun et al. 2016 Mol Psychiatry) is GWAS, not Mendelian. Hence partial: only if FTDP-17 counts as 'very similar' to AD. 4. The 1998 reports (Hutton; Poorkaj; Spillantini) predate the 2018 Phase 2 entry. 5. Not authored by Lilly. No data errors found.

outcome_summary:
ASP8302 is an oral positive allosteric modulator of the muscarinic M3 receptor from Astellas. Its first Phase 2 was NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept study in underactive bladder (UAB). It started on 2018-11-20, enrolled 135 patients, gave 100 mg once daily or placebo for 4 weeks, and completed on 2020-04-28.

The primary endpoint, change in post-void residual volume after standardized bladder filling (PVRc2) at week 4, was missed. The median change was -40 mL on drug versus -35 mL on placebo, a difference of -5 mL (p=0.960). Adverse events were similar between arms (33.3% vs 31.4%).

Target engagement was shown:
- In Phase 1, salivary secretion rose with dose from 100 mg upward, the dose then used in Phase 2.
- In male patients, maximum urine flow rate (Qmax) rose by 3.8 mL/s (p=0.031) and detrusor pressure at Qmax by 12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034). Incontinence episodes also fell in males.

The authors concluded the drug did not work in UAB patients selected by non-urodynamic clinical criteria (PVR above 100 mL). They noted that both baseline flow and voiding pressure were low, and that bladder voiding efficiency measured by ultrasound would have been a better endpoint than PVR.

Astellas's pipeline update of 30 Oct 2020 (Q2 FY2020) states: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint." No Phase 3 or approval followed, and the compound is no longer on Astellas's pipeline page. A 2024 ICI-RS review lists ASP8302 among agents that have shown no unequivocal clinical benefit in detrusor underactivity.

Code F3 was chosen because pharmacology was shown but the benefit appeared only in the male subgroup. The authors attribute the miss to a heterogeneous population chosen without urodynamic testing. F7 is the runner-up, since the authors also faulted PVR as a noisy primary endpoint with a large placebo response.

evidence.earliest_source: Weber S et al., "Muscarinic Acetylcholine Receptor M3 Mutation Causes Urinary Bladder Disease and a Prune-Belly-like Syndrome", Am J Hum Genet 2011 Nov 11;89(5):668-74 (PMID 22077972). The OMIM-submitted ClinVar record VCV000029626 (CHRM3 c.1173_1184delinsT, p.Pro392fs, Pathogenic, Prune belly syndrome, OMIM 118494.0001) cites it and was created 2013-04-04.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: ASP8302 is an Astellas small-molecule positive allosteric modulator of the muscarinic M3 receptor (CHRM3). In cells it shifts the carbachol concentration-response curve leftward at M3 and M5, with no significant effect at other subtypes. It does the same in human bladder strips (Okimoto et al., JPET 2021, PMID 34244231; Takusagawa et al. 2024, PMID 39120583). These papers came out after Phase 2 entry, but they confirm the target and direction recorded in our database.

(2) Entry trial: NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201; EudraCT 2017-003693-13; lead sponsor Astellas Pharma Europe B.V.) is a Phase 2a proof-of-concept study of ASP8302 100 mg against placebo in Underactive Bladder. Inclusion required chronic incomplete emptying with PVR >= 75 mL. Actual start was 2018-11-20, matching the recorded entry date. Mapping it to MONDO:0006026 "urinary bladder disorder" is broad but correct.

(3) Claim: true. Weber 2011 (AJHG) reported a homozygous CHRM3 frameshift in a family with a congenital prune-belly-like syndrome. Cystometry in four affected boys showed "detrusor hyporeflexia with high residual volumes after micturition". Urethral patency was normal, and the boys also had impaired pupil constriction and dry mouth. This is a congenital form of an underactive detrusor with incomplete emptying, so it is a very similar phenotype to UAB. The direction also fits: M3 loss-of-function stops the bladder emptying, and the drug potentiates M3.
- PanelApp lists CHRM3 as Green (confidence 3, biallelic) on panels 156 (Unexplained kidney failure in young people), 234 (CAKUT) and 1537 (Unexplained young onset ESRD - additional genes). The phenotypes are Prune belly syndrome (OMIM 100100), Megacystis and Urinary Bladder Disease. The cited PMIDs are 10944224, 22077972 and 31441039.

CAVEAT on dating: our database dates this evidence to 2000. That year comes from PMID 10944224 (Matsui et al., PNAS 2000, Univ. Tokyo), which describes M3-knockout mice with urinary retention. It is not human germline evidence. The earliest human Mendelian or ClinVar evidence is Weber 2011. The second human family (Beaman et al., Clin Genet 2019, PMID 31441039, homozygous p.Gly118Arg with bladders that fail to empty fully) and its ClinVar record VCV974798 (2020) both came after the 2018-11-20 entry. So before entry, the evidence was a single consanguineous family with a rare congenital disease. The claim still holds, because 2011 and 2013 are both before 2018.

(4) The 2011 paper and the 2013 ClinVar/OMIM record both predate Phase 2 entry. I did not verify when the PanelApp Green ratings were assigned.

(5) Weber 2011 authors are from academic centres only (Essen, Cologne, Bonn, Izmir, Manchester, Aurora, Munster, Mainz, Heidelberg, Munich). Funding was the Wellcome Trust and NIGMS, and Astellas is not mentioned. Matsui 2000 is from the University of Tokyo. Neither is sponsor-authored.

I did not research or report the clinical outcome.

I coded this F2 with moderate confidence. F3 is the main alternative.

Program: ASP8302 (Astellas) is an oral small molecule that boosts the muscarinic M3 receptor (a positive allosteric modulator). It was tested for underactive bladder in NCT03702777, a double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept trial. The trial started 2018-11-20, completed 2020-04-28 with 135 patients enrolled, and gave 100 mg once daily or placebo for 4 weeks. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Why it stopped: Astellas's Q2 FY2020 supplementary results document (published around October 2020) says: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint." The FY2019 Q4 and FY2020 Q1 pipeline tables still list the program as Phase 2, in-house. The Q2 FY2020 presentation moves it to the "Discontinuation" list. No commercial or safety reason is given.

What the trial showed (van Till et al., Neurourol Urodyn 2022, PMID 35419807, abstract only; the full text is behind a paywall):
- Primary endpoint missed. The primary endpoint was the change in urine left in the bladder after voiding (post-void residual, PVR), measured by catheter after standardized filling. The median change was -40 ml on ASP8302 versus -35 ml on placebo, a difference of -5 ml (p=0.960). Voiding efficiency (BVE) was also not different between groups.
- Safety was not the problem. Adverse events were similar in both groups (33.3% vs 31.4%).
- Men responded on secondary measures. Peak urine flow rose by 3.8 ml/s (p=0.031) and bladder-muscle pressure at peak flow rose by 12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034). Incontinence episodes fell.
- The authors' conclusion: patients were selected by "nonurodynamic clinical criteria", there was no efficacy on the primary endpoint, men improved, and BVE is a better outcome measure than PVR.

Was the target engaged? Yes. The Phase 1 studies (PMID 39120583) showed a dose-dependent effect on saliva production "from 100 mg onward", which is an M3-driven effect. That is the dose used in Phase 2a. The rise in bladder-muscle pressure in men shows the drug also acted on the bladder.

Why F2: the drug reached its target at the trial dose and changed bladder physiology, at least in men. Potentiating M3 still did not improve bladder emptying in the overall underactive-bladder population. That is engagement without clinical translation. The failure was not exposure (F1) or toxicity (F5/F6), and the company gave no commercial reason (F8).

Why F3 is close: the abstract stresses that patients were chosen without urodynamic testing, that men responded, and that baseline flow and bladder pressure were low. That could point to the wrong population or disease stage. However, the men-only signal comes from secondary subgroup analyses, and I could not read the full discussion to confirm the authors blame the population.

Endpoint choice (F7) is a lesser contributor. The authors say BVE is a better measure than PVR, but BVE also showed no difference between groups.

adjudication.reasoning:
Outcome: ASP8302 did not advance within 4 years.
- The entry trial NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201; Astellas Pharma Europe) is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept study in underactive bladder. Actual start was 2018-11-20, completion 2020-04-28, with 135 patients enrolled. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.
- A ClinicalTrials.gov search for ASP8302 returns only this trial and the Phase 1 NCT03361540. No Phase 3 exists.
- Astellas's Q2 FY2020 supplementary document, which I downloaded and searched, says: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint."

The pipeline's record is right: s4=0 and the reason is "efficacy: primary endpoint not met". Two labels are slightly off but do not change the outcome:
- The event is coded "suspended" when the program was in fact discontinued.
- years_to_event = 1.44 matches the trial completion date (2020-04-28), not the Oct 2020 announcement.

Trial result (van Till et al., Neurourol Urodyn 2022, PMID 35419807, abstract):
- The primary endpoint, change in post-void residual volume (PVRc2), was missed: -40 mL on drug vs -35 mL on placebo, a difference of -5 mL (p=0.960).
- Adverse events were similar between arms (33.3% vs 31.4%).
- Men improved on secondary measures: peak flow rate (Qmax) +3.8 mL/s (p=0.031), detrusor pressure at Qmax +12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034), and fewer incontinence episodes.
- The authors conclude the drug "did not show efficacy" in patients "identified by nonurodynamic clinical criteria". They note that baseline flow and voiding pressure were low, and that bladder voiding efficiency (BVE) measured by ultrasound is a better endpoint than PVR.

The drug did reach its target:
- In Phase 1 (PMID 39120583), saliva production rose with dose from 100 mg onward, which is the Phase 2 dose.
- In men, detrusor pressure rose in the pressure-flow subgroup.
That rules out F1. Safety was clean, which rules out F5 and F6. Astellas gave efficacy, not strategy, as the reason, which rules out F8.

Failure code: I chose F3 over F2 and F7.
- The primary source explains the miss through the population: a heterogeneous group selected without urodynamics, with low baseline voiding pressure. A positive allosteric modulator can only amplify the cholinergic drive that remains, and the benefit appeared only in men. That is a wrong population or disease subtype.
- F2 is a close second. The genetic evidence is congenital CHRM3 loss of function causing a developmental bladder disease, while the drug potentiates M3 in acquired adult detrusor underactivity, so the biology may not carry over. However, no source makes that argument.
- F7, the noisy PVR endpoint with a large placebo response, contributes but is secondary.

Claim: holds, and the evidence predates entry.
- Weber et al., AJHG 2011 (PMID 22077972) reports a homozygous CHRM3 frameshift in a family with a congenital bladder malformation and prune-belly-like syndrome. I confirmed the PMC full text says cystometry "revealed detrusor hyporeflexia with high residual volumes after micturition", with normal urethral patency. That is a very similar phenotype to underactive bladder, and its direction (M3 loss means failed emptying) fits a drug that potentiates M3.
- The ClinVar record for this variant, VCV000029626 (p.Pro392fs), is Pathogenic for prune belly syndrome (OMIM 100100), last evaluated 2011-11-11.
- Both the paper and the ClinVar record are well before the 2018-11-20 entry.
- Mapping the disease to MONDO:0006026 "urinary bladder disorder" is broad but acceptable.

Minor caveat: our database dates this evidence to 2000. That date comes from Matsui et al. PNAS 2000 (PMID 10944224), a study of M3-knockout mice, not human germline evidence. The correct earliest human date is 2011. This does not change whether the evidence predates entry.

RO7123520 is Roche's RG6125. The EULAR 2019 abstract by Finch et al. describes RG6125 as a humanized anti-cadherin-11 (CDH11) monoclonal antibody. Its trial matches NCT03001219 exactly: 109 patients randomized, 72 on drug and 37 on placebo, 810 mg IV, ACR50 11.1% vs 16.2%. That makes it a CDH11 antibody given on top of patients' existing anti-TNF therapy. Nothing found says it is a bispecific that binds TNF, so the TNF target in the input record is probably the background therapy.

NCT03001219 was Roche's Phase IIa/b trial in RA patients who had responded poorly to anti-TNF therapy and were still taking it with methotrexate. It started on 2016-12-22 and was terminated on 2018-11-06. The stated reason was "a lack of efficacy of the investigational drug"; the record adds that there were "no serious safety issues". Part 3, the dose-ranging part, was never run.

evidence.notes:
1) TARGET AND ACTION. Our record lists RO7123520 as a multispecific antibody that binds and neutralizes both CDH11 and TNF. No source I found supports that format or a TNF arm. The trial is NCT03001219 (Roche protocol BP39261, EudraCT 2016-002126-36). It tests RO7123520 as an add-on for RA patients who continue their existing anti-TNF-alpha therapy and methotrexate. TNF therefore appears in the trial only as background therapy, which is the probable source of the mis-annotation. Roche's own Phase 2 abstract (Finch et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78 Suppl 2:189) describes the study drug, RG6125, as "a novel humanized monoclonal antibody directed against Cadherin-11". That abstract matches NCT03001219 point for point: sponsor Roche; adjunct therapy in anti-TNF-inadequate-responder RA; 4 IV doses up to Week 12 (Days 1, 14, 28 and 56 in the registry); 109 randomized, matching the registry's 109 enrolled. Senolt 2019 (PMC6719675) also describes anti-cadherin-11 RG6125 given on top of anti-TNF therapy. No single source I found states RO7123520 = RG6125 outright; the identity rests on that design match. The EU register gives RO7123520 only as a recombinant biological IV concentrate with no INN.
CDH11 as an antagonist antibody target is consistent. TNF is not a target of the drug, so I marked both target and action "no" for the listed set.

2) DISEASE. The entry trial studied moderately to severely active rheumatoid arthritis, so the mapping is correct.

3) CLAIM. The claim is not supported, for four reasons:
(a) The only evidence row is for TNF, which the drug does not target.
(b) The evidence disease is psoriatic arthritis, not RA. The Open Targets API shows the link only because its ontology lists psoriatic arthritis (MONDO_0011849) as a child of RA (MONDO_0008383). Clinically, psoriatic arthritis is a distinct seronegative arthritis.

Its cited paper (Balding 2003) is a candidate-gene study of the common TNF -308 polymorphism. Coded F1, with low-to-moderate confidence; the borderline case is F2. The program stopped for lack of efficacy, and no source shows that the drug engaged its target in the joint.

What happened: RO7123520 is Roche's RG6125. NCT03001219 (BP39261, EudraCT 2016-002126-36) was a Phase 2 trial in RA patients who had responded inadequately to anti-TNF. The drug was given IV on top of the patients' existing anti-TNF plus methotrexate, and the trial ran from 22 Dec 2016 to 6 Nov 2018.

- **Why it stopped:** ClinicalTrials.gov says the trial "was prematurely terminated due to a lack of efficacy of the investigational drug" and that "there were no serious safety issues or adverse events contributing to the decision." Part 3, the planned dose-ranging part, was never run.
- **Results:** At week 12, ACR50 was 11.1% on 810 mg versus 16.2% on placebo. ACR20 was 27.8% versus 43.2%. DAS28 fell by 1.15 versus 1.62 and CDAI by 14.4 versus 17.4. Anti-drug antibodies were 0%.
- **Same drug, two names:** The EULAR 2019 abstract OP0224 (Finch et al., Roche) describes the identical trial: 109 patients randomized 2:1 (72 drug, 37 placebo), 810 mg IV, 4 doses to week 12, primary endpoint ACR50. That is how RG6125 is identified as RO7123520. The abstract concludes the drug "did not show a discernible treatment effect", with only mild-to-moderate adverse events.
- **Later reviews:** Senolt 2019 (PMC6719675), Németh et al. 2022 (PMC9279838) and a 2024 review (PMC11112866) all record the reason as lack of efficacy. The last says the trial was discontinued in 2018.

- Blood levels of the drug were shown: the abstract reports that RG6125 pharmacokinetics "appears linear", with "no significant relationship" between exposure group and efficacy at week 12.
- No marker showing cadherin-11 was actually blocked was reported, and the drug was never shown to reach or act in the joint. Drug concentration in synovial fluid was a planned secondary endpoint. ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU register say neither serum nor synovial-fluid concentrations were analyzed "due to an insufficient number of available participant samples." That contradicts the abstract's PK statement and is unresolved.
- F2 requires engagement to have been shown, and no source shows it. The flat exposure-response at a high dose is ambiguous: the target may have been saturated, or the drug may never have engaged it in the joint.
- F3 is possible but no source states it: the population was anti-TNF-refractory with a median disease duration of 12.4 years. F5/F6 are ruled out by the sponsor's statement on safety. F8 is not suggested by any source.

Data correction for our records: the abstract describes RG6125 as "a novel humanized monoclonal antibody directed against Cadherin-11". The record's "multispecific_antibody" modality and its TNF target are probably wrong. The TNF inhibitor was background therapy that patients were already taking, not part of the drug.

Unclear: when Roche formally removed the drug from its pipeline. I found no Roche press release or pipeline document.

The pipeline recorded s4=0, reason "efficacy: stated" and an event at 1.87 years, which matches 2016-12-22 to 2018-11-06. That outcome is correct. Calling the event "suspended" rather than "terminated" is a minor wording difference that changes nothing.

DRUG IDENTITY AND TARGET. The EU register lists RO7123520 only as a recombinant biological IV concentrate (30 mg/ml) with no INN. Finch et al., EULAR 2019 OP0224 (Roche authors), describes RG6125 as "a novel humanized monoclonal antibody directed against Cadherin-11". Its numbers match the CT.gov results exactly: 109 randomized (72 drug, 37 placebo), 810 mg IV, 4 doses up to week 12, ACR50 11.1% vs 16.2%, ACR20 27.8% vs 43.2%. On that match, RO7123520 = RG6125, an anti-CDH11 monoclonal antibody. No source supports a TNF arm. TNF appears in the trial only as background therapy, listed as the "Anti-TNF-alpha" intervention in every arm, including placebo. The "multispecific_antibody" modality and the TNF binder_neutralizer target are therefore mislabels.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Jeunemaitre X, Soubrier F, ... Lifton RP, ... Lalouel JM. "Molecular basis of human hypertension: role of angiotensinogen." Cell 1992 Oct 2;71(1):169-80 (PMID 1394429). This is the UniProt P01019 evidence for "Essential hypertension (EHT), MIM 145500", alongside Ward et al. Nat Genet 1993 on preeclampsia (PMID 8513325).
outcome_summary:
Evazarsen (IONIS-AGT-LRx, ISIS 757456) is Ionis's GalNAc-conjugated antisense drug that lowers hepatic angiotensinogen (AGT). Its first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial in hypertension was NCT03714776 (n=25, controlled hypertension), which started on 2019-01-03. That trial met its primary endpoint, AGT reduction: -54% vs +13% on placebo, p<0.001. In-clinic systolic blood pressure (SBP) did not differ from placebo at any visit. A second Phase 2, NCT04083222 (n=26, uncontrolled hypertension, started Nov 2019), reduced AGT by 67%, again with no consistent SBP separation. The Ionis paper on these trials (JACC BTS 2021, PMID 34222719) says they were not powered for blood pressure and showed only "trends".

The trial that decided the program was the Phase 2b NCT04714320 (n=160, uncontrolled or treatment-resistant hypertension, 80 or 120 mg weekly for 12 weeks; started 2021-04-28, primary completion 2022-06-29). Its primary endpoint, change in seated automated office SBP at Day 85, failed. The least-squares mean changes were -13 mmHg (80 mg) and -9 mmHg (120 mg) vs -9 mmHg on placebo, with p=0.135 and p=0.867. Plasma AGT fell by about 60% at both doses. Twenty-four-hour ambulatory SBP was also not significant (p=0.094 and 0.842). Safety did not limit the drug: serious adverse events were 2/54 on 80 mg and 1/53 on 120 mg vs 1/53 on placebo.

Ionis listed a Phase 2b readout for H2 2022 (Q2/Q3 2022 8-Ks), but its 10-K filed Feb 2023 described the trial without giving any results. The 10-K filed Feb 2024 no longer lists IONIS-AGT-LRx as a program. It mentions the drug only as the reference for the follow-on AGT drug ION904, which is designed for less frequent dosing. Results for NCT04714320 were not posted on ClinicalTrials.gov until Feb 2025. No later trials or Phase 3 exist.

Ionis never published a reason for stopping. Efficacy is my inference: the program was dropped after a failed SBP primary endpoint and replaced by a next-generation molecule. That is primarily an efficacy failure with a portfolio substitution (F8 element). I chose F2 because the drug clearly engaged its target (about 60% AGT knockdown) but this partial knockdown did not lower blood pressure. F4 is a reasonable alternative, since the AGT biomarker moved while the clinical BP endpoint did not.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: confirmed. IONIS-AGT-LRx (ISIS 757456) is an antisense inhibitor of angiotensinogen (AGT) that lowers AGT levels. Sources are the NCT03714776 title ("an Antisense Inhibitor") with its AGT/angiotensinogen keywords, and the Ionis-authored Morgan et al., JACC BTS 2021 (PMID 34222719). That paper was used only for mechanism.

(2) Entry trial: confirmed. NCT03714776 is a Phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled study sponsored by Ionis. Its condition is "Mild Hypertension" in hypertensive participants whose blood pressure is controlled. Actual start 2019-01-03, which matches the Phase 2 entry date. Mapping it to MONDO:0005044 "hypertensive disorder" is appropriate, and the evidence disease, essential hypertension, is a subtype.

(3) Claim: partly supported. A curated germline gene-disease link did exist before Phase 2:
- UniProt P01019 lists "Essential hypertension" with the note "Disease susceptibility is associated with variants affecting the gene", citing PMID 1394429 (1992) and PMID 8513325 (1993, preeclampsia).
- Jeunemaitre 1992 reported sib-pair linkage, an association of M235T/T174M with hypertension, and higher plasma AGT by genotype.

But this is complex-trait susceptibility evidence, not Mendelian or ClinVar-pathogenic:
- ClinVar VCV000018068 (rs699, M235T) for "Hypertension, essential, susceptibility to" (RCV000019691) was "risk factor" in 2016 and "Benign, risk factor" from 2018-05-29. So at entry in Jan 2019 it was never classified pathogenic.
- OMIM has since reclassified M235T as a polymorphism (Hamosh 2024, using gnomAD allele frequency of about 0.47).
- ClinVar's pathogenic/likely pathogenic AGT variants are tied to renal tubular dysgenesis, a loss-of-function disease, not hypertension.

So "curated" is true, but "Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic" overstates it.

(4) Timing: the 1992 source predates the 2019-01-03 entry by about 26 years.

(5) Sponsor authorship: no. The authors were academic groups (HHMI/University of Utah and INSERM Paris), and Ionis had no part in the paper.

Ionis never published a reason for stopping, so the code rests on the trial results plus the program's quiet removal from Ionis's filings.

Program: evazarsen (IONIS-AGT-LRx, ISIS 757456), an Ionis liver-targeted antisense drug that cuts AGT production, for hypertension. Phase 2 began 2019-01-03 with NCT03714776. No Phase 3 has been registered: a ClinicalTrials.gov search on all code names returns one Phase 1 and four Phase 2 trials.

1) The target was engaged in every trial (ClinicalTrials.gov results):
- NCT03714776 (n=25, mild hypertension): AGT fell 54.2% by Day 43, versus a 12.6% rise on placebo (p<0.001). Office systolic pressure did not differ from placebo (e.g. Day 8 p=0.909, Day 15 p=0.132).
- NCT04083222 (n=26, uncontrolled hypertension): AGT fell 67.4% versus 3.4% on placebo (p<0.001). Systolic pressure did not differ (p=0.21-0.40 at early visits).
- Ionis's own paper (Morgan et al., JACC Basic Transl Sci 2021, PMID 34222719) says the drug "significantly reduced AGT" but the trials were "not powered" for blood pressure, with only "trends" seen.

2) The decisive Phase 2b trial missed its primary endpoint. NCT04714320 enrolled 160 patients with treatment-resistant hypertension on 3 or more drugs, and ran from April 2021 to October 2022.
- AGT fell 54-64% by Days 29-43 (p<0.001).
- The primary endpoint was the change in seated office systolic pressure at Day 85: placebo -9, 80 mg -13 (p=0.135), 120 mg -9 (p=0.867) mmHg. The higher dose did no better than the lower one.
- 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure was also not significant (80 mg p=0.094, 120 mg p=0.842).
- No safety signal stood out: serious adverse events were 1/53 on placebo, 2/54 at 80 mg and 1/53 at 120 mg.

3) What Ionis's filings show:
- The FY2021 10-K still described the earlier "trends" in blood pressure.
- The Q3 2022 8-K listed the Phase 2b readout for 2022.
- The FY2022 10-K (filed February 2023) described the Phase 2b design but reported no blood-pressure result. It only said the drug lowered AGT and was well tolerated.
- The FY2023 10-K (filed February 2024) drops IONIS-AGT-LRx entirely. Only ION904 remains: "a follow-on medicine targeting AGT, designed to enable less frequent dosing compared to IONIS-AGT-LRx."
- The heart-failure Phase 2 (NCT04836182) completed in January 2023 but has posted no results.

Why F2 and not the alternatives:
- F2 fits because plasma AGT is a direct measure of target engagement, and partial liver AGT knockdown (about 55-65%) did not produce clinical blood-pressure lowering.
- F4 (biomarker moved, outcome didn't) fits less well. AGT is the drug's own target, not a disease surrogate, and the blood-pressure endpoint itself failed.
- F8 (replaced by ION904) is a plausible secondary code, since ION904's Phase 2 started in April 2022, before this readout. Ionis gave no strategic reason, though, and the failed efficacy trial is the documented event that came before the program was dropped.

Caveats: Ionis made no explicit discontinuation statement, so the causal link is inferred from the timing. "Partial inhibition" as the mechanism is my interpretation, not a stated finding.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Stoy J et al., "Insulin gene mutations as a cause of permanent neonatal diabetes", PNAS 2007;104(38):15040-4 (PMID 17855560). It is the earliest publication cited by the PanelApp panel 293 (Neonatal diabetes) INS entry that Open Targets maps to type 1 diabetes. A closer Mendelian link to clinically diagnosed T1D is Molven A et al., Diabetes 2008 (PMID 18192540): INS R55C in autoantibody-negative T1D. OMIM and ClinVar classify that variant as Pathogenic for "Type 1 diabetes mellitus 2". The common-variant IDDM2/INS-VNTR association with T1D dates to Bell et al., Diabetes 1984 (PMID 6363172), but it is not Mendelian.
outcome_summary:
TOL-3021 (formerly BHT-3021, from Bayhill Therapeutics and then Tolerion) is an intramuscular DNA plasmid that encodes human proinsulin. It is meant to induce antigen-specific tolerance in type 1 diabetes. Phase 2 entry is confirmed: SUNRISE (NCT03895437) is a randomized (2:1), triple-blind, placebo-controlled, industry-sponsored (Tolerion) Phase 2 trial that started on 2019-06-17. It enrolled 78 people aged 12-40 who were within 5 years of diagnosis.

SUNRISE was terminated, with primary completion on 2020-12-21. The registry states: "The DSMB concluded that there was a low probability the study would meet its primary endpoint as designed." The DSMB ran an interim analysis once at least 30 TOL-3021 subjects had reached Week 24. The primary endpoint was change from baseline in log-transformed MMTT C-peptide AUC, analysed by repeated measures at Weeks 12, 16 and 24. TOL-3021 and placebo did not differ:
- Week 24: -0.06 for TOL-3021 vs -0.05 for placebo.
- MMRM p=0.368.
The posted results say the drug "showed no efficacy relative to placebo". All 51 TOL-3021 and 27 placebo participants were withdrawn for "Lack of Efficacy". There were no serious adverse events in either arm, so safety was not the reason for stopping. The two planned Phase 2b follow-on trials (DAY, NCT03794960; DAWN, NCT03794973) were withdrawn before enrollment, citing "Modification to Clinical Development Plan". No Phase 3 has ever been registered, and there has been no approval, so the program did not advance within 4 years and appears to be stopped.

Failure code F2: engagement was shown, but the biology did not translate. The Phase 1/2 study (Roep et al., Sci Transl Med 2013) found that proinsulin-reactive CD8+ T cells fell selectively (P<0.006), with only a transient C-peptide signal at the 1 mg dose (Week 15, P<0.026). The adequately controlled Phase 2 then showed no preservation of beta-cell function.

Caveats:
- SUNRISE did not report a mechanistic or engagement biomarker, so engagement during Phase 2 itself is not documented. F4 (the biomarker moved but the clinical outcome did not) is a reasonable alternative code.
- I found no company press release or SEC filing about the termination. The web-search budget was exhausted, and tolerion.com redirects to a sign-in page. The stop reason therefore rests on the ClinicalTrials.gov record, whose posted results list PBM Capital Group as the contact.

It is the earliest publication cited by the PanelApp panel 293 (Neonatal diabetes) INS entry that Open Targets maps to type 1 diabetes. A closer Mendelian link to clinically diagnosed T1D is Molven A et al., Diabetes 2008 (PMID 18192540): INS R55C in autoantibody-negative T1D. The common-variant IDDM2/INS-VNTR association with T1D dates to Bell et al., Diabetes 1984 (PMID 6363172), but it is not Mendelian.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target/action. TOL-3021 (formerly BHT-3021) is a bacterial plasmid that encodes human proinsulin (hINS), according to the intervention description on CT.gov NCT03895437. It is an antigen-specific tolerising DNA vaccine meant to reduce proinsulin-specific CD8+ T cells (Roep et al., Sci Transl Med 2013, PMID 23803704, authored by Bayhill/Tolerion). INS is the encoded antigen and is not inhibited or activated, so the action "other" is correct.
(2) Disease. NCT03895437 (sponsor Tolerion; Phase 2; start 2019-06-17, matching the entry date) enrolled new-onset or established type 1 diabetes, condition "Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1". The mapping is correct.
(3) Claim. The DB row is Genomics England PanelApp panel 293, "Neonatal diabetes". There INS is Green (level 3), with phenotype "Diabetes mellitus, insulin-dependent, 2, 125852" (OMIM IDDM2), which Open Targets maps to MONDO_0005147. The panel cites PMIDs 17855560 (Stoy 2007, PNDM) and 26101329 (Carmody 2015, intronic INS mutation causing neonatal-onset diabetes). INS was already Green with the IDDM2 and T1D phenotype strings in panel v1.0 (version_created 2017-11-05).
ClinVar also has OMIM-submitted Pathogenic assertions under "TYPE 1 DIABETES MELLITUS 2". One is INS c.163C>T p.Arg55Cys (VCV000013392), citing Molven 2008: a girl and her mother with ketoacidosis-onset, GAD/IA-2 antibody-negative "type 1" diabetes. The other is p.Gly32Ser (VCV000021122), a PNDM allele from Stoy 2007, which a University of Chicago lab submitted as IDDM2 in 2014.
So curated Mendelian and ClinVar-pathogenic evidence linking INS to a label that MONDO and OMIM treat as a T1D subtype exists, and it predates 2019. I rate it "partial" because every Mendelian INS diabetes is monogenic, autoantibody-negative, insulin-deficient diabetes (PNDM, MODY10, antibody-negative T1D), caused by proinsulin misfolding and beta-cell ER stress. It is not the autoimmune T1D the trial treats. The only genetic link to autoimmune T1D is the common IDDM2 INS-VNTR susceptibility locus (Bell 1984; Bennett et al., Nat Genet 1995, PMID 7773291). That is association evidence, not Mendelian, although it is mechanistically relevant to proinsulin tolerance.
(4) All of these sources (1984, 1995, 2007, 2008, 2015; PanelApp 2017) predate 2019-06-17.
(5) None of the genetics papers were authored by Bayhill Therapeutics or Tolerion; their authors are at the University of Chicago, Exeter, Bergen and Oxford. Only the Phase 1 trial paper (Roep 2013) is sponsor-authored, and it is not the genetic evidence.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: TOL-3021 (formerly BHT-3021), a bacterial plasmid that encodes human proinsulin. It was given as a weekly intramuscular injection to tolerize proinsulin-reactive T cells in type 1 diabetes. Sponsor: Tolerion, Inc.

Why it did not advance (primary sources):
1) The Phase 2 entry trial, SUNRISE (NCT03895437), started 2019-06-17. It randomized 78 patients aged 12 to <41 within 5 years of diagnosis 2:1 to drug or placebo for 52 weeks. It is TERMINATED. ClinicalTrials.gov gives the reason as "The DSMB concluded that there was a low probability the study would meet it is primary endpoint as designed." The results population note says the interim analysis came after at least 30 TOL-3021 subjects reached Week 24, and "The DSMB determined that the investigational drug showed no efficacy relative to placebo and recommended termination." Limitations field: "Early termination following interim analysis showing lack of efficacy." All 78 participants are listed as not completed, with "Lack of Efficacy" as the reason.
2) Primary endpoint numbers (change in log MMTT C-peptide AUC, MMRM, p=0.368): Week 12, -0.04 vs -0.03; Week 24, -0.06 vs -0.05, drug vs placebo. Secondary endpoints also showed no benefit: HbA1c p=0.109 (numerically worse on drug), insulin dose p=0.146, hypoglycemia p=0.976.
3) Safety was not the cause. There were no SAEs or deaths, no severe related AEs, and only 3 related TEAEs (injection-site pain or hypoaesthesia, headache).
4) The two follow-on Phase 2b trials, DAY (NCT03794960) and DAWN (NCT03794973), were WITHDRAWN with 0 enrolled. Their stated reason is "Modification to Clinical Development Plan", last updated 2020-12-08, which is when SUNRISE ended (2020-12-21). No other TOL-3021 trial appears on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Why F2 rather than another code: engagement of the intended mechanism had been shown before Phase 2. In the Phase 1/2a trial (Roep et al., Sci Transl Med 2013, PMID 23803704; NCT00453375), BHT-3021 lowered proinsulin-reactive CD8+ T cells but not T cells against other islet or viral antigens (P<0.006). The same trial reported a C-peptide gain at the 1 mg dose at Week 15 (+19.5% vs -8.8%, P<0.026). The SUNRISE protocol (v1.07) cites this antigen-specific CD8 reduction as its rationale, keeps the 1 mg weekly dose and lengthens dosing to 52 weeks. In the adequately controlled Phase 2, this antigen-specific immune modulation did not turn into preserved beta-cell function: C-peptide was the same as placebo. That fits F2: engagement shown, biology did not translate.

Why not the alternatives:
- F5 and F6 are ruled out by the clean safety data.
- F8 is ruled out because the DSMB futility finding came first; the withdrawal of DAY and DAWN followed from it and was not a separate portfolio decision.
- F7 is not supported. The trial used the best Phase 1 dose for longer, with a pre-specified O'Brien-Fleming interim analysis, and no source blames design or power.
- F3 is not supported. The population matched the Phase 1 trial (diagnosed within 5 years, autoantibody-positive) with adolescents added, and no source blames population.
- F4 is not chosen because SUNRISE reported no biomarker that moved. C-peptide, the accepted efficacy endpoint, did not move.

Caveats (marked unclear):
- Whether TOL-3021 engaged its target within SUNRISE is unclear. The protocol planned Q-dot multimer CD8+ T-cell assays (section 13.3.5), but no immunology results were posted or published.
- No source explains mechanistically why the effect did not translate. The small, multi-dose Phase 1 C-peptide signal may simply have been a false positive, which would point more toward F1/F2 ambiguity.
- No Tolerion press release or paper on SUNRISE was found. tolerion.com now redirects to an unrelated sign-in page, and the Wayback Machine has only a 2018 homepage. The WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted, so the press-release search was limited to direct fetches.
- Confidence in F2 over F1 is moderate.

evidence_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-5678895 'Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis' (disease: cystic fibrosis; reaction R-HSA-5678822 'Defective CFTR does not transport Cl-'), released 2015-06-17 (Reactome v53)
stop_reason: n/a (approved)
outcome_summary:
The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of elexacaftor (VX-445) in CF is Vertex's Phase 1/2 study NCT03227471 (VX-445-001), actual start 2017-01-23, matching the pipeline date. Its Part D/E/F cohorts in CF patients showed ppFEV1 gains of ~11-14 points with the VX-445/tezacaftor/ivacaftor triple versus ~0 for placebo or TEZ/IVA (CT.gov posted results).

Vertex started Phase 3 on 2018-06-15 (NCT03525444, F508del/minimal function, vs placebo) and 2018-08-03 (NCT03525548, F/F vs TEZ/IVA). Both met their primary ppFEV1 endpoints (Middleton et al., NEJM 2019; Heijerman et al., Lancet 2019). FDA approved Trikafta on 2019-10-21 for CF patients aged 12 and older with at least one F508del allele, and has since widened the label to younger children and more mutations.

The program advanced well within 4 years and is approved for the disease.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
error_source: DATA ERROR: the entity is OCTA12 (a VWF fragment), whose molecular identity is VWF-derived; recording F8 as its target conflates the excipient-like VWF fragment with the FVIII component of OCTA101.
evidence_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-9662001 'Defective factor VIII causes hemophilia A' (with child pathways R-HSA-9672397 Defective F8 secretion, R-HSA-9672391 cleavage by thrombin, R-HSA-9672393 binding to VWF, etc.), all with releaseDate 2020-06-10 (Reactome release 73) per Reactome ContentService.
stop_reason: Phase 1/2 terminated due to serious adverse drug reactions: unexpectedly high incidence of FVIII inhibitors (5/30, 16.7%) with subcutaneous OCTA101; clinical development discontinued
outcome_summary:
OCTA12 is a recombinant human VWF fragment dimer used as a FVIII chaperone; it was developed clinically only as a component of OCTA101 (OCTA8 rhFVIII + OCTA12) for subcutaneous prophylaxis. The only industry trial is NCT04046848 (Octapharma, Phase 1/2, severe hemophilia A, previously treated adults), actual start 2019-07-03, matching the pipeline date.

The study was terminated (ClinicalTrials.gov whyStopped: 'Study was terminated due to SADRs'). The published report (PubMed 37975434) states FVIII inhibitors developed in 5 of 30 treated patients (16.7%) during daily SC prophylaxis, prompting discontinuation of OCTA101 development. No Phase 3 was started. Primary endpoints were descriptive safety counts (AEs, DLTs, inhibitor formation), so 'met/not met' does not apply; the safety outcome was the reason for stopping.

Failure code F6: molecule/formulation-specific immunogenicity (inhibitor development with the SC FVIII/VWF-fragment product), not a failure of the replacement biology itself.

evidence.earliest_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-9662001 'Defective factor VIII causes hemophilia A' (with child pathways R-HSA-9672397 Defective F8 secretion, R-HSA-9672391 cleavage by thrombin, R-HSA-9672393 binding to VWF, etc.), all with releaseDate 2020-06-10 (Reactome release 73) per Reactome ContentService.
evidence.notes:
1. OCTA12 is Octapharma's recombinant human von Willebrand factor (VWF) fragment dimer; it has no hemostatic function itself and is combined with human-cl rhFVIII (OCTA8) as OCTA101 to raise FVIII bioavailability after subcutaneous dosing. The program (NCT04046848, Phase 1/2, start 2019-07-03 ACTUAL, sponsor Octapharma) delivers FVIII, so F8 as the functional target and 'increases function' are defensible for the combination, but OCTA12's direct binding partner is FVIII via a VWF fragment (gene VWF), not an F8 gene product.
DATA ERROR: the entity is OCTA12 (a VWF fragment), whose molecular identity is VWF-derived; recording F8 as its target conflates the excipient-like VWF fragment with the FVIII component of OCTA101.
2. Hemophilia A (MONDO:0010602) mapping is correct.
3. Reactome's F8 disease content (Diseases of hemostasis R-HSA-9671793; Defective factor VIII causes hemophilia A R-HSA-9662001 and its six child pathways, reactions such as R-HSA-9661980, R-HSA-9665809) was all first released 2020-06-10. No earlier Reactome disease event involving F8 was found via the ContentService search. Before that, F8 appeared only in normal coagulation pathways.
4. 2020-06-10 is after the 2019-07-03 Phase 2 entry, so the 'before Phase 2' condition fails; the claim is not supported (the curation exists today but postdates entry).
5. Reactome curation is not sponsor-authored.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome R-HSA-2219530 'Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer' (released 2012-09-18; disease: cancer) includes MET only as one of the activated RTKs upstream of mutant PI3K. No pre-2015 Reactome disease entity where MET itself is perturbed was found.
stop_reason: Sanofi gave no public reason. The only Phase 2 trial (NCT02435121, MET-amplified NSCLC) enrolled 1 patient and closed in January 2016, about 2 months after starting. AdisInsight lists the drug as discontinued for NSCLC and solid tumours. With n=1, no efficacy or safety readout could have driven the stop, which suggests a sponsor or portfolio decision, but this is not documented.
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT02435121 is Sanofi's open-label single-arm Phase 2 of weekly IV SAR125844 (a selective MET kinase inhibitor) in pretreated NSCLC with MET amplification. It started in November 2015 (month only), with primary completion in January 2016 (actual). Actual enrollment was 1, and no ORR results are posted. It is the only Phase 2 trial of the agent on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Advancement: no Phase 3 trial or approval followed. The preceding Phase 1 trials (NCT01391533, Angevin et al., Eur J Cancer 2017, PMID 29145039; NCT01657214, Shitara et al., Oncotarget 2017, PMID 29108334) set 570 mg/m2 weekly as the MTD/recommended dose. They reported partial responses in 4 of 22 MET-amplified NSCLC patients and modest activity in MET-amplified gastric cancer, so the molecule did show clinical activity.

Status: development was discontinued (AdisInsight; Patsnap Synapse). We found no Sanofi statement explaining why the Phase 2 closed after one patient. A strategic or portfolio decision, or a feasibility problem in a rare biomarker population, are both plausible, but neither is documented, so the failure code is 'unknown' (F8 most likely).

evidence.earliest_source: Reactome R-HSA-2219530 'Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer' (released 2012-09-18; disease: cancer) includes MET only as one of the activated RTKs upstream of mutant PI3K. No pre-2015 Reactome disease entity where MET itself is perturbed was found.
evidence.notes:
1. SAR125844 (Sanofi) is a selective MET kinase inhibitor; target MET and 'decreases function' are correct.
2. MONDO:0004992 'cancer' is very broad. The Phase 2 program was in MET-amplified NSCLC / MET-amplified solid tumours, so 'cancer' is acceptable but imprecise.
3. Reactome maps MET (UniProt P08581) to just two disease-flagged pathways: R-HSA-2219530 'Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer' (2012) and R-HSA-8875360 InlB-mediated Listeria entry (an infection). In R-HSA-2219530 the perturbed entities are PIK3CA/PIK3R1 gain-of-function mutants. MET appears only as a wild-type activated RTK, so MET is not the perturbed gene product the claim requires.
4. The Reactome pathway that describes oncogenic MET amplification/mutation, R-HSA-9734091 'Drug-mediated inhibition of MET activation', was released 2021-09-15, after the 2015-11-01 Phase 2 entry, and is not disease-flagged.
5. Verdict: a cancer disease pathway containing MET predates entry (hence partial). A curated MET-perturbation disease reaction does not.
6. No data errors found.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-5678895 'Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis' (disease tag: cystic fibrosis), first released 2015-06-17
stop_reason: Inhaled CFTR mRNA was safe and well tolerated, but the multiple-ascending-dose cohorts showed no pattern of ppFEV1 improvement (second interim, March 2021). The early single-dose FEV1 signal from 2019 did not replicate. Translate Bio shifted to a next-generation CF candidate before Sanofi acquired it in 2021, and MRT5005 was dropped.
outcome_summary:
NCT03375047 (RESTORE-CF) is a Phase 1/2 trial of nebulized MRT5005 in adults with CF. It was initiated by Translate Bio and is now listed under Sanofi. The actual start was 2018-05-10, matching the pipeline date, and it completed 2022-03-15 with 42 enrolled and results posted. Its primary endpoint, treatment-emergent and serious adverse events, was met: dosing was generally safe and tolerated. On efficacy, the 2019 interim showed ppFEV1 increases after a single dose, but the March 2021 second interim found 'no pattern of increases in ppFEV1' in the multiple-dose groups.

No Phase 3 followed. Translate Bio redirected to a next-generation CF mRNA/LNP candidate, Sanofi bought the company in 2021, and the CF Foundation lists MRT5005 as discontinued. I code F1: no study showed that the molecule delivered enough functional CFTR protein to the airway epithelium. There was no lung-expression or CFTR-function biomarker, and the sponsor's move to a next-generation delivery candidate points to a delivery or expression problem with this molecule, not a failure of CFTR biology (which CFTR modulators validate). F2 is less likely.

evidence.earliest_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-5678895 'Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis' (disease tag: cystic fibrosis), first released 2015-06-17
evidence.notes:
1. MRT5005 is an inhaled, lipid-nanoparticle-formulated mRNA encoding CFTR (Translate Bio). It delivers functional CFTR, so target CFTR and action 'increases target function' are correct.
2. MONDO:0009061 cystic fibrosis (OMIM 219700) is the correct indication.
3. Reactome ContentService gives R-HSA-5678895 'Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis' with releaseDate 2015-06-17 and disease = cystic fibrosis. It curates mutant CFTR (e.g. F508del) failing ER folding/trafficking, a direct perturbation of the target's gene product in this exact disease. This predates the Phase 1/2 entry (2018-05-10) by about 3 years.
4. Reactome is an independent curation (OICR/EBI/NYU), not Translate Bio/Shire.
5. No data error found.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-8862803 'Deregulated CDK5 triggers multiple neurodegenerative pathways in Alzheimer's disease models' with APP reactions R-HSA-8870710 'APP gene expression' (increased via FOXO3) and R-HSA-8863009 (beta-amyloid-driven Ca2+ influx), disease = Alzheimer's disease, released 2016-09-19
stop_reason: not_stopped
outcome_summary: Eli Lilly's anti-amyloid antibody donanemab (LY3002813) entered Phase 2 in Alzheimer's disease with TRAILBLAZER-ALZ (NCT03367403). That trial started on 2017-12-18 and completed. It met its primary endpoint, change from baseline in iADRS, with a difference of 3.20 and p=0.042 (ClinicalTrials.gov results; Mintun et al., NEJM 2021). The Phase 3 trial TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (NCT04437511) started on 2020-06-19, well inside the 4-year window. It met its primary iADRS endpoint at week 76 in the overall population (2.92, p<0.0001, per FDA; Sims et al., JAMA 2023). The FDA approved Kisunla (donanemab-azbt) for Alzheimer's disease under BLA 761248 on 2024-07-02, for patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia. Drugs@FDA also lists an efficacy supplement approved on 2025-07-01. The program advanced and is approved, so it is not a failure.

evidence.earliest_source: Reactome pathway R-HSA-8862803 'Deregulated CDK5 triggers multiple neurodegenerative pathways in Alzheimer's disease models' with APP reactions R-HSA-8870710 'APP gene expression' (increased via FOXO3) and R-HSA-8863009 (beta-amyloid-driven Ca2+ influx), disease = Alzheimer's disease, released 2016-09-19
evidence.notes:
1. Donanemab binds N-terminal pyroglutamate amyloid-beta (AbetaN3pG) in deposited plaque; amyloid-beta is an APP cleavage product, so APP is the right gene but the true target is a modified APP fragment, not APP protein itself (partial).
DATA ERROR: recorded action 'addresss' is a malformed/garbled action string; the correct action is that the antibody binds and clears plaque amyloid-beta (i.e. decreases/removes the target species).
2. MONDO:0004975 Alzheimer disease is the correct disease.
3. Reactome disease-tagged reactions with APP/beta-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease (isInDisease=true, disease 'Alzheimer's disease') were released 2016-09-19, about 15 months before Phase 2 entry (2017-12-18). Earlier, 2011-06-14 reactions in 'Amyloid fiber formation' (R-HSA-977136, R-HSA-976734) carry disease 'Amyloidosis' and include amyloid-beta fibril formation, but are not AD-specific. Caveat: the AD pathway is curated from mouse 'AD models' (Shi et al. 2016), but it is tagged to the human disease.
4. Reactome is not authored by Eli Lilly.
5. The Reactome reaction R-HSA-9939011 (lecanemab binds Abeta protofibrils) is a 2026 addition and does not count.

The industry-sponsored Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04693520 is an open-label biomarker study by Alzheon of ALZ-801 in APOE4 carriers with early Alzheimer's disease. It started on 2020-09-30 (actual), and ClinicalTrials.gov lists it as COMPLETED.
