stop_reason: n/a. The drug is approved and marketed only in Japan (IZCARGO, 2021). The global Phase 3 STARLIGHT is active, not recruiting, and in October 2026 JCR licensed US, EU and LatAm rights to Italfarmaco to pursue FDA, EMA, MHRA and ANVISA approval.
outcome_summary:
The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of pabinafusp alfa (JR-141) in MPS II is NCT03128593, a Phase 1/2 study in 14 Japanese patients sponsored by JCR Pharmaceuticals. ClinicalTrials.gov records its actual start as 2017-03-30, matching the pipeline date. A Brazilian Phase 2 trial (NCT03359213) followed in July 2018.

JCR started the Japanese Phase 2/3 study NCT03568175 on 2018-08-01. It was single-arm, enrolled 28 patients and was completed 2020-02-20. Its primary endpoint was change in cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate, which fell significantly, as published by Okuyama et al. in Mol Ther 2021. On that basis Japan approved the drug as IZCARGO in 2021. A Phase 2/3 start counts as a Phase 3 start, so the program advanced within 4 years. The caveat is that the global randomized Phase 3 STARLIGHT (NCT04573023) started 2022-02-14, about 4.9 years after entry, and that there is no FDA approval.

Now: pabinafusp alfa is marketed in Japan. STARLIGHT is active, not recruiting; JCR announced in July 2025 that enrollment was complete. On 2026-10-02 JCR and Italfarmaco signed an exclusive license for the US, Europe and Latin America, aimed at FDA, EMA, MHRA and ANVISA approvals.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome reactions 'SARS-CoV-2 N binds NLRP3' (R-HSA-9757097) and 'SARS-CoV-2 3a induces potassium efflux' (R-HSA-9730521) within 'SARS-CoV-2 activates/modulates innate and adaptive immune responses' (R-HSA-9705671), releaseDate 2022-03-23. Reactome's SARS-CoV-2 Infection pathway (R-HSA-9694516) itself was first released 2020-09-15.
stop_reason: Single Phase 2 (DFV890D12201) completed Dec 2020 without meeting its primary endpoint; Novartis did not pursue COVID-19 further and redirected DFV890 to other NLRP3 indications (FCAS, knee OA, CHD/CHIP, myeloid diseases).
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT04382053 (DFV890D12201), Novartis-sponsored randomized open-label Phase 2 of DFV890 + standard of care vs SoC alone in COVID-19 pneumonia with impaired respiratory function, actual start 2020-05-27, completed 2020-12-24 (ClinicalTrials.gov). It is the only industry trial of DFV890 in COVID-19.

No Phase 3 or approval followed. The primary endpoint, APACHE II score at Day 15/discharge (worst-case imputation for death), was 8.7 with DFV890 vs 8.6 with SoC (ANCOVA p=0.467) per posted results; the publication (Madurka et al., Infection 2023, PMC9473473; n=70 vs 72) reports no significant superiority on the primary endpoint, with directional benefits on viral clearance, clinical status and mechanical-ventilation-free survival on secondary/exploratory measures and good tolerability.

Code F2: an oral NLRP3 inhibitor was dosed with acceptable tolerability (and is being advanced in other inflammatory indications, implying adequate exposure), yet inflammasome inhibition did not translate into a primary clinical benefit in COVID-19 pneumonia. The rapid evolution of COVID-19 standard of care (dexamethasone) and a waning pandemic may also have contributed to the decision not to continue, but no explicit stop statement was found.

1. DFV890 (Novartis) is an oral NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitor; target NLRP3 and 'decreases target function' are correct.
2. COVID-19 (MONDO:0100096) matches NCT04382053, 'Study of Efficacy and Safety of DFV890 in Patients With COVID-19 Pneumonia', Phase 2, start 2020-05-27 ACTUAL.
3. Reactome had no COVID-19 content at all before the 2020-05-27 entry: the earliest COVID-19-tagged events date from 2020-09-15 (e.g., R-HSA-9694572), and the SARS-CoV-2 Infection pathway was first released 2020-09-15. The first COVID-19 events that involve NLRP3 (N binds NLRP3; 3a-induced K+ efflux feeding NLRP3 activation) were released 2022-03-23. claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome R-HSA-2023837 'Signaling by FGFR2 amplification mutants' and parent R-HSA-5655253 'Signaling by FGFR2 in disease' (release date 2012-06-12): FGFR2 amplification in ~10% of gastric cancers (Hattori 1996; Kunii 2008) and activating somatic FGFR2 mutations in gastric cancer.
stop_reason: FIDES-03 terminated (primary completion 2022-11-21) 'for administrative reasons not related to patient safety' after Basilea exited oncology and returned derazantinib rights to Merck & Co. by end-2022, citing a competitive landscape and evolving open-label clinical data. Posted monotherapy results were weak (ORR 0% in cohorts 1.1/1.2; PFS4 7.7% in cohort 1.3).
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry: FIDES-03 (NCT04604132), Basilea's Phase 1b/2 study of derazantinib alone or with paclitaxel/ramucirumab or atezolizumab in HER2-negative FGFR2-aberrant gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, has actual start 2020-10-06, matching the pipeline. No earlier industry Phase 2 in gastric cancer was registered (earlier trials were the solid-tumor Ph1/2 NCT01752920, iCCA FIDES-01, urothelial FIDES-02).

Outcome: The trial enrolled 47 and was terminated. Posted results on ClinicalTrials.gov show ORR 0% (upper 95% CI 20.6% and 31.2%) in monotherapy cohorts 1.1 and 1.2 at 300 mg QD, and PFS at 4 months of 7.7% in cohort 1.3 (200 mg BID); the combination substudy only established an RP2D of 200 mg. Basilea announced in 2022 it would return derazantinib rights to Merck & Co. by year-end, citing an inability to meet license terms amid a competitive landscape and evolving open-label data, as part of its exit from oncology.

Classification: drug was dosed to/above prior effective iCCA levels (including an intensified 400 mg/day exploration), yet monotherapy showed no responses in FGFR2-aberrant gastric cancer, so F2 (biology did not translate) best fits, with a commercial overlay (F8) in the formal termination.

evidence.earliest_source: Reactome R-HSA-2023837 'Signaling by FGFR2 amplification mutants' and parent R-HSA-5655253 'Signaling by FGFR2 in disease' (release date 2012-06-12): FGFR2 amplification in ~10% of gastric cancers (Hattori 1996; Kunii 2008) and activating somatic FGFR2 mutations in gastric cancer.
evidence.notes:
1. Derazantinib (ARQ 087; ArQule/Basilea) is an ATP-competitive pan-FGFR (FGFR1-3) kinase inhibitor, with secondary activity on CSF1R/VEGFR2. Target and 'decreases function' are correct.

Outcome: The trial enrolled 47 and was terminated. failure_second.rationale: FIDES-03 (NCT04604132, start 2020-10-06, n=47, terminated 'for administrative reasons') posted ORR 0% in both 300 mg QD monotherapy cohorts (1.1 and 1.2) and PFS4 7.7% in the intensified 200 mg BID cohort 1.3. claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, Reactome had curated a disease reaction or pathway in which the target's gene product is perturbed in this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease).
evidence_source: Reactome 'Signaling by NOTCH1 in Cancer' sub-pathways, e.g. R-HSA-2894862 'Constitutive Signaling by NOTCH1 HD+PEST Domain Mutants' with reactions R-HSA-2769000/R-HSA-2900747 'NOTCH1 ... mutants bind DLL4' (disease: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia; cancer), released 2012-03-12
stop_reason: The Phase 2 in metastatic colorectal cancer was stopped after an interim analysis showed no efficacy gain over bevacizumab. Dilpacimab plus FOLFIRI was worse on PFS and ORR and was poorly tolerated. AbbVie then discontinued clinical development.
outcome_summary:
Dilpacimab (ABT-165) is AbbVie's DLL4/VEGF dual-variable-domain antibody. Its only Phase 2 is NCT03368859, which compared dilpacimab plus FOLFIRI with bevacizumab plus FOLFIRI in second-line metastatic colorectal cancer. It actually started on 2018-03-20 (matching the pipeline date) and was terminated on 2019-12-18. The other trial of the drug is the Phase 1 solid-tumor study NCT01946074.

The primary endpoint was PFS. Posted results show median PFS of 3.78 months on dilpacimab against 7.36 months on bevacizumab, ORR of 5.6% against 14.7%, and median OS of 7.95 months against not reached. There were 12 of 34 deaths on dilpacimab against 6 of 32 on bevacizumab, and 17 against 8 SAEs. The publication (Future Oncology 2022, doi 10.2217/fon-2021-1603) says the study was stopped after an interim analysis showed no efficacy gain beyond bevacizumab. It also says dilpacimab plus FOLFIRI was not well tolerated and that the sponsor has discontinued development. No Phase 3 or approval followed.

The Phase 1 showed adequate exposure, but adding DLL4 blockade gave no benefit and worse tolerability, so this is coded F2. F5 (toxicity offsetting efficacy) is a possible alternative.

evidence.notes:
1. Dilpacimab (ABT-165) is an AbbVie DLL4/VEGF dual-variable-domain immunoglobulin that blocks both ligands; targets DLL4+VEGFA and action 'decreases' are correct.
2. MONDO:0004992 'cancer' is very broad; the program was in advanced solid tumours with Phase 2 in metastatic colorectal cancer, so the mapping is acceptable but non-specific (partial).
3. DLL4 appears in Reactome disease reactions released 2012-03-12 (isInDisease=true; disease T-ALL and cancer), but only as the wild-type ligand that binds oncogenic NOTCH1 HD/PEST mutants; the perturbed gene product is NOTCH1, not DLL4, and the disease is T-ALL rather than solid tumours. VEGFA (P15692) participates in 56 Reactome reactions, none of them disease-tagged. So no Reactome entry shows either target's own product perturbed in a solid cancer: partial support at most.
4. Reactome is not AbbVie-authored.
5. No data error found in target, action or the Phase 2 date checked.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Olaparib (Lynparza tablets, AstraZeneca), NDA 208558 (supplemental approval), approved 2019-12-27 as maintenance treatment of adults with germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma that has not progressed on at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum chemotherapy (POLO trial)
stop_reason: The Phase 3 trial NCT04300114 was terminated on 2022-02-18 after enrolling 5 patients. The stated reason is 'Sponsor R & D Strategy Adjustment'. No FDA or other approval for pancreatic cancer was found, and no later Phase 3 in this disease is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.
outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04228601 is a Phase 1b/2 trial of fuzuloparib plus mFOLFIRINOX in advanced pancreatic cancer, sponsored by Jiangsu Hengrui. Its actual start date is 2020-01-21, which matches the recorded date. It enrolled 39 patients and completed in January 2023. The Phase 2 primary endpoint was objective response rate.

The program advanced within 4 years. Hengrui started the Phase 3 maintenance trial NCT04300114 (fuzuloparib vs placebo after first-line platinum, PFS by central review) on 2020-08-19.

The Phase 3 was terminated on 2022-02-18 with only 5 patients enrolled. The registry gives the reason as a sponsor R&D strategy adjustment, so the stop was a business decision and no efficacy readout exists. Fuzuloparib is approved in China for ovarian cancer, but no approval or active late-stage development in pancreatic cancer was found. Because the program reached Phase 3 inside the window, it counts as advanced, even though the pancreatic program later stopped for commercial reasons.

evidence.notes: 1. Fuzuloparib (fluzoparib, SHR-3162, Jiangsu Hengrui) is a small-molecule PARP1/PARP2 inhibitor. The recorded targets PARP1+PARP2 and the action 'decrease' are correct. 2. Its start date of 2020-01-21 matches the recorded entry date, and the MONDO term 'malignant pancreatic neoplasm' fits this trial and Hengrui's later pancreatic trials: NCT04300114 (Phase 3, gBRCA/PALB2 maintenance) and NCT04425876 (resectable disease). 3. The FDA approved it for gBRCAm metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma on 2019-12-27, 25 days before Phase 2 entry, so the precedent is for the same disease. Olaparib's first-ever FDA approval was the capsule form for ovarian cancer (NDA 206162, 2014-12-19), but that was a different disease. The earliest approval that qualifies here is the 2019 pancreatic one. 4. Olaparib is sponsored by AstraZeneca/Merck, not Hengrui, so sponsor_authored is 'no'. 5. The supplement number for the pancreatic approval is not verified: I could not open the approval letter (404), and the date and indication come from trade and professional press reports of the FDA action.

Its earliest industry Phase 2 in breast cancer is NCT04165993 (KN026 alone or in combination in HER2-expressing/positive metastatic breast cancer), actual start 2019-12-31, matching the pipeline date. Earlier breast-cancer trials (NCT03619681, NCT03847168) are Phase 1. A neoadjuvant Phase 2 (NCT04881929) followed in 2021. An HR+ combination study (NCT04778982) was terminated for slow enrollment.

The first breast-cancer Phase 3, NCT05838066, sponsored by Shanghai JMT-Bio, started on 2023-07-23. It tests KN026 + HB1801 (albumin-bound docetaxel) against trastuzumab + pertuzumab + docetaxel as first-line treatment, with BIRC-assessed PFS as primary endpoint. That start falls inside the 4-year window, which ends 2023-12-31. More Phase 3s followed: neoadjuvant (NCT06747338, Dec 2024) and adjuvant (NCT07441460, first patient dosed March 2026 per Alphamab). No Phase 3 breast-cancer results are posted, and there is no FDA approval.

The program advanced to Phase 3 within 4 years and remains active.

evidence.earliest_source: FDA approval of trastuzumab (Herceptin, BLA 103792) for HER2-overexpressing metastatic breast cancer, 25 Sep 1998
evidence.notes:
1. Anbenitamab (KN026, Alphamab) is a HER2 biparatopic antibody binding ECD2 and ECD4 and blocking HER2 signalling; target ERBB2 and action 'decreases' are correct.
2. Breast cancer MONDO:0007254 is a sound mapping (programme is in HER2-positive breast cancer, a subtype).
3. FDA approved trastuzumab (1998), lapatinib (2007), pertuzumab (2012), ado-trastuzumab emtansine (2013) and neratinib (2017) for HER2-positive breast cancer, all acting on ERBB2.
4. The earliest, trastuzumab in 1998, long predates the 2019-12-31 Phase 2 entry. Genentech is not the sponsor. No data errors found.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Jakafi (ruxolitinib phosphate, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor), NDA 202192, approved 2011-11-16 for intermediate- or high-risk myelofibrosis
stop_reason: Business decision. In June 2022 Roivant/Dermavant discontinued DMVT-502 (topical cerdulatinib, for vitiligo and atopic dermatitis), along with DMVT-503 and DMVT-504, to put its resources into the launch of VTAMA (tapinarof), which the FDA approved in May 2022. outcome_summary:
Entry trial: NCT04103060, a Phase 2a sponsored by Dermavant Sciences GmbH. It was randomized, double-blind and vehicle-controlled, testing cerdulatinib gel 0.37% in adults with vitiligo. Actual start was 2019-09-27, which matches the recorded entry date, and actual completion was 2020-11-03, with 33 patients enrolled. The primary endpoints were safety and tolerability only: vital signs, lab values, adverse events and local tolerability through Week 7. Secondary endpoints were plasma cerdulatinib levels and blister-fluid biomarkers. The registry has no posted results and was last updated in November 2020.

What happened next: no Phase 3 of cerdulatinib in vitiligo followed, from any sponsor. On 2022-06-28 BioSpace reported that Roivant's Dermavant had stopped developing DMVT-502 (vitiligo and atopic dermatitis), DMVT-503 and DMVT-504 so it could focus on launching VTAMA. Cerdulatinib is DMVT-502, per Dermavant's cerdulatinib topical patent and other public references. Separately, Portola withdrew the systemic oncology Phase 2b, CELTIC-1 (NCT04021082), as a 'sponsor decision to not initiate'. Dermavant was later acquired by Organon, and the program has not come back.

Why it stopped: the stated reason is a portfolio reprioritization, so the code is F8. No vitiligo efficacy data were disclosed, so it is unknown whether weak biology also played a part. One source is unreliable here: the VRF pipeline summary puts cerdulatinib under the code 'DMVT-504' and says it was deprioritized 'before entering trials'. That conflicts with the registry and with the BioSpace report, so it was not relied on.

evidence.earliest_source: Jakafi (ruxolitinib phosphate, a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor), NDA 202192, approved 2011-11-16 for intermediate- or high-risk myelofibrosis
evidence.notes: 1) Cerdulatinib is described as a dual SYK/JAK inhibitor that inhibits SYK, JAK1, JAK3 and TYK2. The recorded targets and the 'decrease' direction match that description; I did not open a source for this point in this session. 2) The program's Phase 2 trial is NCT04103060, 'Safety and Tolerability Study of Cerdulatinib Gel, 0.37% in Adults With Vitiligo'. It is a Phase 2 trial sponsored by Dermavant Sciences GmbH, it started on 2019-09-27 and its condition is vitiligo, so the MONDO:0008661 mapping and the entry date are right. 3) The first FDA-approved drug that acts on a recorded target is ruxolitinib (Jakafi, NDA 202192), which inhibits JAK1. It was approved on 2011-11-16 for myelofibrosis, well before Phase 2 entry. Other JAK and SYK drugs, such as tofacitinib (2012, rheumatoid arthritis), baricitinib (2018, rheumatoid arthritis) and fostamatinib (2018, ITP), were also approved before 2019, but none of them for vitiligo or a skin disease. 4) The first approval of a JAK inhibitor for a skin disease is Opzelura (topical ruxolitinib, NDA 215309): 2021-09-21 for atopic dermatitis and 2022-07-18 for vitiligo. Both dates come after the 2019-09-27 entry, so at entry the only target precedent was for clearly different diseases (myeloproliferative and rheumatologic), which makes the claim partial. 5) The precedent drugs belong to Incyte, Pfizer, Lilly and Rigel, not to Dermavant or Portola, so sponsor_authored is no.

failure_second.rationale: Dermavant's only vitiligo trial was a Phase 2a study, NCT04103060 (DMVT-502-2101). It was a small safety, tolerability and systemic-exposure study: 33 adults received cerdulatinib 0.37% gel or vehicle twice daily for 6 weeks. ClinicalTrials.gov shows no posted results. The sponsor said top-line results were due in the second half of 2020, but I found no press release or publication reporting efficacy or a safety problem. Roivant's 2021 pipeline still listed topical cerdulatinib at Phase 2 for vitiligo and atopic dermatitis. In June 2022 Roivant said Dermavant was 'closing out the development of DMVT-502 for vitiligo and atopic dermatitis' (BioSpace, 2022-06-28). It gave one reason: Dermavant was moving its resources to launching VTAMA (tapinarof) after its FDA approval for psoriasis. That is a strategic portfolio stop, so the code is F8. This is the only reason on record. Because the Phase 2a efficacy data were never made public, an undisclosed weak efficacy signal (F2), or a 6-week trial too short to show repigmentation (F7), cannot be ruled out. Confidence in F8 is therefore moderate.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
error_source: DATA ERROR: The recorded Phase 2 entry is the start of a combined Phase 1/2 trial whose posted results cover only dose-escalation cohorts at 0.25-3 mg. No Phase 2 expansion part was ever reported, so this is not a true Phase 2 start.
evidence_source: Lenalidomide (Revlimid), NDA 021880 supplement S-034, approved 2013-06-05 for relapsed/progressive mantle cell lymphoma after two prior therapies including bortezomib. CRBN-acting drugs approved earlier were only for other diseases: thalidomide (NDA 020785) on 1998-07-16 for erythema nodosum leprosum, lenalidomide (NDA 021880) on 2005-12-27 for del(5q) MDS and in 2006 for multiple myeloma.
stop_reason: No reason is stated. NCT02406742 completed on 2020-07-07 with only its dose-escalation arms enrolled (46 participants of 47 enrolled). Its Phase 2 part was never run, and no later CLL trial was registered. Single-agent activity was weak (best overall response 7.1%, 1/14). Celgene/BMS then took avadomide forward in DLBCL, HCC and melanoma, not CLL. No sponsor statement on the CLL program was found.
outcome_summary:
The entry trial is NCT02406742 (CC-122-CLL-001), a Celgene-sponsored, later BMS, Phase 1/2 open-label dose-finding study of CC-122 alone (Arm A), with ibrutinib (Arm B) and with obinutuzumab (Arm C) in CLL/SLL. Its actual start was 2015-07-27, which matches the recorded date. The disease mapping to CLL (MONDO:0004948) is correct.
DATA ERROR: The recorded Phase 2 entry is the start of a combined Phase 1/2 trial whose posted results cover only dose-escalation cohorts at 0.25-3 mg. No Phase 2 expansion part was ever reported, so this is not a true Phase 2 start.

The primary endpoints were safety and NTD/MTD. Neither the NTD nor the MTD was reached in the combination arms. Single-agent CC-122 had a best overall response of 7.1% (1/14), and discontinuations were mainly for progression (5) and adverse events (3). Response was 87.5% with ibrutinib and 62.5% with obinutuzumab, but those partners are active in CLL on their own, and bone-marrow MRD negativity was 0% in every arm. The study completed on 2020-07-07, and results were posted in 2021.

No Phase 3 trial in CLL or SLL followed, and no reason for stopping has been published. The weak single-agent activity is consistent with F2, but no source attributes the stop to it, and a portfolio decision (F8) is just as plausible. The code is therefore unknown.

evidence.earliest_source: Lenalidomide (Revlimid), NDA 021880 supplement S-034, approved 2013-06-05 for relapsed/progressive mantle cell lymphoma after two prior therapies including bortezomib. CRBN-acting drugs approved earlier were only for other diseases: thalidomide (NDA 020785) on 1998-07-16 for erythema nodosum leprosum, lenalidomide (NDA 021880) on 2005-12-27 for del(5q) MDS and in 2006 for multiple myeloma.
evidence.notes: 1. Target: avadomide (CC-122) is a cereblon-modulating drug (CELMoD). It binds CRBN, the substrate receptor of the CRL4 ubiquitin ligase, and makes it degrade Ikaros and Aiolos (IKZF1/3). CRBN is the correct target. 2. Action: 'ambiguous' is defensible but only partly right. The drug changes which proteins CRBN targets (a molecular glue that gains a new function); it does not simply increase or decrease CRBN function. Thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide work the same way, so the direction matches the precedent drugs. 3. Disease: the entry trial is NCT02406742 (Celgene, Phase 1/2, CC-122 with ibrutinib and obinutuzumab in CLL/SLL). It started 2015-07-27, which matches the recorded entry date, and MONDO:0004948 B-cell CLL fits. 4. Precedent: no CRBN modulator was approved for CLL before entry. Lenalidomide's mantle cell lymphoma approval (2013-06-05) is the closest one before entry. MCL and CLL/SLL are both CD5-positive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so I counted MCL as closely related and marked the claim 'yes'. That is a judgment call. If MCL is treated as a different disease, the answer becomes 'partial': the earliest CRBN precedent is then thalidomide for ENL in 1998, or lenalidomide for myeloma and MDS in 2005-2006. 5. Sponsor: lenalidomide (Revlimid) and thalidomide (Thalomid) are Celgene drugs, and Celgene also sponsored avadomide's entry trial, so sponsor_authored is 'yes'.

outcome.advance_event: none; ClinicalTrials.gov lists no Phase 3 trial of avadomide (CC-122) in CLL from any sponsor, and the FDA has not approved it for any indication

failure_second.rationale: 1. NCT02406742 (CC-122-CLL-001) is a Phase 1/2 trial in relapsed/refractory CLL/SLL. It started on 2015-07-27 and had three dose-escalation arms: avadomide alone, avadomide plus ibrutinib, and avadomide plus obinutuzumab. Its primary endpoints were safety and the maximum tolerated dose, not efficacy. 2. Protocol Amendment 7 (protocol document dated 2018-07-27) records that on 05 Jul 2018 Celgene told all sites it was ending development of CC-122 in CLL once the Phase 1 dose-escalation part finished. The Phase 2 expansion cohorts (50 and 40 patients per cohort were planned) never enrolled. The sponsor wrote that 'the decision was not based on adverse safety findings, and no new safety signals for CC-122 have been identified.' Patients who were benefiting could stay on treatment for up to 24 cycles. 3. Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov cover 46 treated patients at doses of 0.25 to 3.0 mg. None completed the study. Withdrawals for disease progression were 5, 1 and 6 in the three arms, and withdrawals for adverse events were 3, 0 and 2. No efficacy endpoint was reported, and I found no published CLL efficacy data. So neither a missed endpoint nor a toxicity signal is on record. 4. The sponsor ruled out safety and stopped the CLL indication across all three arms before efficacy was formally tested. Over the same period Celgene kept developing avadomide in DLBCL and other non-Hodgkin lymphomas. That fits a portfolio or strategic stop (F8) better than F2, F5 or F6. Caveat: Celgene never gave a positive reason. Weak signs of efficacy in the escalation cohorts could have contributed, and if a stated reason is required, 'unknown' is the alternative code.

adjudication.rationale: The Amendment 7 protocol for NCT02406742 (https://cdn.clinicaltrials.gov/large-docs/42/NCT02406742/Prot_000.pdf, dated 27 Jul 2018) says in its Protocol Summary: 'On 05 Jul 2018, Celgene informed all study sites that further development of CC-122 in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) will be discontinued after completion of the current Phase 1 Dose Escalation Phase. Enrollment into the Phase 2 Dose Expansion Phase will not proceed forward as originally planned. The decision was not based on adverse safety findings, and no new safety signals for CC-122 have been identified.' The trial started 2015-07-27 and is listed as COMPLETED on 2020-07-07, with no whyStopped entry. So a sponsor statement exists, and Coder A's 'no sponsor statement' is wrong. The statement closes the CLL program as a development decision and rules out safety (F5/F6). The posted results do not make this an efficacy failure either. Single-agent BOR was low at 7.1% (Arm A), but the combinations were 87.5% with ibrutinib (Arm B) and 62.5% with obinutuzumab (Arm C). Those combination rates likely owe much to the partner drugs, and Phase 2 was never run to test any of it. With the efficacy question left open, a sponsor stop that names no safety cause is a portfolio stop, coded F8, which matches Celgene continuing avadomide in DLBCL. Caveat: the statement does not exclude weak single-agent activity as one reason for the decision, so F2 may have contributed, but the documented cause is the sponsor's decision.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
error_source: DATA ERROR: the disease is too broad. The first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial is NCT02959918 (Selecta, started October 2016, which matches the recorded entry date). It enrolled people with symptomatic gout and high blood uric acid. Later trials (NCT03905512 Phase 2; NCT04513366 and NCT04596540 Phase 3) are in chronic gout refractory to conventional therapy. The better term is gout (MONDO:0005393). In MONDO, the recorded term MONDO:0037829 'purine metabolism disease' has only 'inborn disorder of purine metabolism' as a child, and gout's ancestors run through 'metabolic disease', not through this term. Gout is still closely related to purine and urate metabolism, so the mapping is partial.
evidence_source: Krystexxa (pegloticase, Savient), BLA 125293, approved 2010-09-14, for chronic gout in adults refractory to conventional therapy
stop_reason: not stopped
outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry trial is NCT02959918, Selecta Biosciences' multi-dose safety and pharmacodynamic study of SEL-212 (pegadricase plus ImmTOR/SEL-110, nanoencapsulated sirolimus) in symptomatic gout with elevated uric acid. It started in October 2016 (actual) and completed in January 2019, which confirms the recorded entry date of 2016-10-01. It followed the Phase 1 trial NCT02648269, which started in December 2015.

Sobi licensed SEL-212 and ran two Phase 3 trials. DISSOLVE I (NCT04513366) started on 2020-08-18, inside the 4-year window. DISSOLVE II (NCT04596540) started on 2020-11-30, just outside it. Both met their primary endpoint of serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL for at least 80% of month 6, with response rates of 56% and 47% at the 0.15 mg/kg dose. Sobi began a rolling BLA in July 2024 under Fast Track designation. The FDA accepted the BLA for NASP (the renamed SEL-212) with a PDUFA date of 2026-06-27.

On 2026-06-26 the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter that cited only manufacturing control strategy and deficiencies at a third-party contract manufacturer. It raised no concerns about efficacy or safety. The program is therefore unapproved but still in development. Note on the disease field: the recorded MONDO:0037829 (purine metabolism disease) is a broad parent term. Every trial was in gout, specifically chronic refractory or uncontrolled gout, so the mapping is acceptable but coarse. This is not a data error.

evidence.earliest_source: Krystexxa (pegloticase, Savient), BLA 125293, approved 2010-09-14, for chronic gout in adults refractory to conventional therapy
evidence.notes:
1. Pegadricase (pegsiticase, SEL-037) is a PEGylated recombinant uricase. It is the enzyme component of SEL-212, which is given with SEL-110 (ImmTOR) to block anti-drug antibodies. It adds urate oxidase activity, which humans lack, so the action 'increase' is right. The target is only partly confirmed because HGNC lists human UOX (HGNC:12575) as a unitary pseudogene. The drug supplies the enzyme activity the human gene no longer makes; it does not act on a human UOX protein. Approved uricases are conventionally mapped to UOX, so the mapping is usable.
2. DATA ERROR: the disease is too broad. The first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial is NCT02959918 (Selecta, started October 2016, which matches the recorded entry date). It enrolled people with symptomatic gout and high blood uric acid. Later trials (NCT03905512 Phase 2; NCT04513366 and NCT04596540 Phase 3) are in chronic gout refractory to conventional therapy. The better term is gout (MONDO:0005393). In MONDO, the recorded term MONDO:0037829 'purine metabolism disease' has only 'inborn disorder of purine metabolism' as a child, and gout's ancestors run through 'metabolic disease', not through this term. Gout is still closely related to purine and urate metabolism, so the mapping is partial.
3. Pegloticase (Krystexxa, BLA 125293) is also a PEGylated uricase. The FDA approved it on 2010-09-14 for chronic gout in adults refractory to conventional therapy, which is the same disease that SEL-212 later targeted in its Phase 3 trials. That is about 6 years before the October 2016 Phase 2 entry, so the claim is supported.
4. An earlier uricase approval exists: rasburicase (Elitek, BLA 103946), approved 2002-07-12 to manage plasma uric acid in children with leukemia, lymphoma or solid tumours receiving anti-cancer therapy. That is hyperuricemia linked to cancer treatment, a related condition but not gout. So pegloticase is the earliest approval for the same disease, and rasburicase is the earliest approval on the target for any use.
5. Neither precedent drug belongs to the sponsor. Pegloticase was Savient's (now Horizon/Amgen) and rasburicase is Sanofi's; Selecta and Sobi own neither.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
error_source: DATA ERROR (possible): 2019-05-30 is the start of Kintor's first ClinicalTrials.gov-registered Phase 2, but it may not be the first industry-sponsored Phase 2. Kintor ran mCRPC trials in China outside ClinicalTrials.gov: its China Phase 3 in mCRPC started May 2018, and Phase 2 trials in China came before that. So the true Phase 2 entry is probably 2018 or earlier. The exact China Phase 2 start date is unknown from the sources I checked. The B1 conclusion stands either way, because flutamide's 1989 approval comes before any of these dates.
evidence_source: Flutamide (EULEXIN, Schering), NDA 018554, approved 1989-01-27 (new molecular entity) for metastatic prostate cancer, given with an LHRH agonist; later AR-antagonist approvals for prostate cancer include bicalutamide (1995), nilutamide (1996) and enzalutamide (2012)
key_trial: China Phase III, proxalutamide monotherapy in 2L+ mCRPC (Kintor; no NCT number; probably CDE registration CTR20180849, which could not be opened to confirm)
stop_reason: The China monotherapy Phase III missed its interim rPFS analysis (IDMC, September 2020) and its final OS co-primary endpoint (announced 2023-03-28). Kintor blamed a heavily pretreated population (>90% had both abiraterone and docetaxel), small sample size and alpha spent at the interim. No topline for the abiraterone combination Phase III was found. Kintor's 2024 annual report shows it gave up proxalutamide and effectively closed its oncology R&D (funding and strategy).
outcome_summary:
DATA ERROR: The recorded Phase 2 entry date (2019-05-30) is the start of NCT03899467, a US open-label Phase II (Kintor; 61 patients with mHSPC or mCRPC after abiraterone or enzalutamide; 400 vs 500 mg; primary endpoint safety and choice of the Phase II dose). It is the first industry Phase II on ClinicalTrials.gov but not the first in this disease. Kintor's own timeline says its China Phase II in prostate cancer launched in 2015, and its China Phase III trials launched in 2017-2018. The program's Phase 2 entry should be about 2015. The disease (prostate cancer, mCRPC) is correct.

The program reached Phase III. evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. In the Merck discovery paper (Jones et al., J Med Chem 2009, PMID 19873981), niraparib (MK-4827) inhibits PARP1 with an IC50 of 3.8 nM and PARP2 with an IC50 of 2.1 nM.

(2) The entry trial is NCT02854436 (Galahad), a Phase 2 study of niraparib monotherapy in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and DNA-repair anomalies. Its condition is listed as "Prostatic Neoplasms", its sponsor is Janssen R&D, and its actual start date is 2016-08-31, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. So the disease mapping to prostate cancer is correct.

(3) The claim is only partly supported:
- **What holds:** an FDA-approved drug acting on the same targets (PARP1/PARP2) existed before Phase 2 entry. This was olaparib, approved for germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer. openFDA gives the original approval status date as 20141219, and the letter's electronic signature is dated 12/19/2014, which matches the evidence rows' 2014-12-19.
- **What fails:** that approval was for ovarian cancer, not prostate cancer. Ovarian cancer is a different organ and sex-specific cancer, not a closely related disease. The only link is the shared BRCA/homologous-recombination-deficiency biomarker logic.
- No PARP inhibitor was approved for prostate cancer before entry. openFDA shows rucaparib's prostate efficacy supplement on 2020-05-15 and olaparib's on 2020-05-19 (FDA mCRPC letter, 208558 S-014). Rucaparib's first approval was 2016-12-19 and niraparib's was 2017-03-27, both after entry.
- If the benchmark counts ovarian cancer as "closely related" to prostate cancer, the claim holds. Otherwise the same-target approval exists, but the disease part of the claim is not met.

(4) The approval (2014-12-19) predates Phase 2 entry (2016-08-31) by about 20 months.

(5) The approval belongs to AstraZeneca, the olaparib sponsor. The niraparib entry trial was sponsored by Janssen, and niraparib originated at Merck. So the key evidence was not authored by the drug's sponsor.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Cymbalta (duloxetine HCl, Eli Lilly), NDA 021733, approved 2004-09-03 (Lilly announced it 2004-09-07) for the management of diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain. Duloxetine inhibits serotonin reuptake through SLC6A4 (and also NET).
stop_reason: No stated reason. Both Angelini Phase 2 trials missed their primary pain endpoints: NCT03202979, low-dose trazodone added to gabapentin (2017-2018), and NCT03749642, the trazodone/gabapentin fixed-dose combination (2018-2020). The 2024 paper on the second trial calls the lowest dose (2.5/25 mg) the best candidate for further development. No later trial is registered, so the program looks dormant or stopped.
outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry trial is NCT03202979, sponsored by Angelini. Its actual start date was 2017-05-16, which matches the recorded entry date. It was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot in 141 patients with painful diabetic neuropathy who all took open-label gabapentin. They received trazodone 10 mg or 20 mg three times a day, or placebo, for 8 weeks. The primary endpoint, the change in BPI-SF item 5, was not met: -3.1, -2.6 and -2.5 for the two trazodone doses and placebo. The 10 mg arm showed only a trend (p=0.118). The authors called for adequately powered confirmatory trials (Lipone et al., CNS Drugs 2020).

Angelini then developed a low-dose trazodone/gabapentin fixed-dose combination. A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers established dose proportionality and found no pharmacokinetic interaction between the two drugs. The Phase 2 dose-finding trial NCT03749642 randomized 240 patients and ran from 2018-11 to 2020-06. Its primary endpoint, the change in the NRS pain score at week 8, was also not met. Placebo improved by -2.02, the three combination doses by -2.24 to -2.52, and gabapentin alone by -1.92. The lowest dose separated from placebo only at week 6. No Phase 3 trial had started by 2021-05-16, the end of the 4-year window, and none is registered as of 2026.

No source gives a reason for stopping. The coding is F7 because placebo response was large, about -2 points on an 11-point scale, in both trials. The gabapentin reference arm did no better than placebo, which shows the trial could not detect even a known active drug. Both studies were small pilot or dose-finding designs. A true lack of efficacy at these very low trazodone doses (F2 or F1) cannot be excluded.

failure_second.rationale: The entry trial, NCT03202979 (started 2017-05-16, completed 2018-08, n=141), tested low-dose trazodone (10 or 20 mg three times daily) as an add-on to open-label gabapentin. It missed its primary endpoint, the change in BPI-SF item 5 at week 8: TRZ30 -3.1, TRZ60 -2.6, placebo -2.5 (TRZ30 vs placebo p=0.118). Only nominal secondary signals favoured the drug (BPI item 6 p=0.031, 50% responders 62.8% vs 45.8%). Angelini then ran a dose-finding Phase 2 of a trazodone/gabapentin fixed-dose combination, NCT03749642 (n=240 mITT). It also missed its primary endpoint, change in NRS pain at week 8. The linear dose-contrast test was not significant, and no dose differed from placebo on Dunnett tests: 2.5/25 mg -2.52, 5/50 mg -2.24, 10/100 mg -2.46, placebo -2.02 (p=0.15, 0.59, 0.45). Only a post-hoc week-6 difference for the lowest dose was significant. In two consecutive sponsor trials the drug did not separate from placebo on the clinical endpoint. Neither showed a dose-response: the lowest dose did best and higher doses did no better. Exposure was not limiting. Trazodone's pharmacology is well characterised, the doses were chosen on purpose from a translational PK/PD model, and the drug caused CNS effects and QT prolongation. Safety was acceptable, with no related serious adverse events, so this is not F5 or F6. No sponsor document gives a commercial stop reason, and no Phase 3 or approval followed. The 2024 paper only says the lowest dose 'may be' a candidate for further development. The placebo response was large (about -2 to -2.5 points), and the pilot study was small and not powered for confirmation, so F7 is a credible secondary reading. But the drug failed twice, including in a larger trial with a placebo arm of 83 patients, and the absent dose-response points to an effect that did not translate to patients. F2 is the better primary code.

adjudication.rationale: I agree with Coder A. Neither trial can tell us whether the drug works, so the failure belongs to the trial design rather than the biology. (1) NCT03202979 (start 2017-05-16, n=142, about 47 per arm) was a pilot of trazodone 30 or 60 mg/day added on top of open-label gabapentin. Pain (BPI-SF item 5) fell by -3.1 at 30 mg, -2.6 at 60 mg and -2.5 on placebo, with no significant difference (30 mg vs placebo p=0.118). Every arm, placebo included, improved substantially (Lipone 2020, CNS Drugs, PMID 32936427). (2) NCT03749642 (n=240, about 38 per active arm) was a dose-finding trial of the trazodone/gabapentin combination with a gabapentin-alone arm included to check that the trial could detect a known drug. Pain (11-point NRS) fell by -2.52, -2.24 and -2.46 in the three combination arms, -1.92 on gabapentin alone and -2.02 on placebo. Gabapentin did no better than placebo. The authors write that this assay-sensitivity check 'did not reveal differences between gabapentin and placebo', and they call the sample 'underpowered' and 'probably insufficient to demonstrate the primary endpoint' (Tesfaye 2024, Pain Ther, PMID 38914876, PMC11255147). (3) A trial in which an established treatment for this disease cannot beat placebo has no assay sensitivity. Its null result is therefore not evidence that the biology failed, and that undercuts Coder B's F2. The reversed dose-response (lowest dose best) appears in noisy, small arms of under 40 patients, and it does not show that trazodone reached its target without moving the disease. (4) The second trial was not a separate large test: it was a 240-patient, five-arm study with about 38 patients per active arm. The two misses come from two underpowered pain trials with high placebo response, not two adequate tests of the drug. Neither registry entry gives a reason for stopping. The sponsor's 2024 paper still names the lowest dose as the best candidate for further development, so no Phase 3 followed but nobody stated that the biology had failed. If anything, a portfolio decision (F8) is a better runner-up than F2.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Desipramine (Norpramin), NDA 014399, original approval 1964-11-20, for depression (a tricyclic that blocks norepinephrine reuptake, SLC6A2). A cleaner single-transporter precedent is fluoxetine (Prozac, Eli Lilly), NDA 018936, approved 1987-12-29 for depression (blocks serotonin reuptake, SLC6A4).
stop_reason: Otsuka's FY2022 results (Feb 14, 2023) say development for MDD in Japan 'was halted due to development strategy', after the Phase 2 trial missed its primary endpoint (MADRS week 6, 20 mg vs placebo -1.1, 95% CI -3.3 to 1.0, p=0.288)
outcome_summary:
The entry trial is NCT04244253, Otsuka's Phase 2 trial of OPC-64005 in major depressive disorder in Japan. It started on 2020-03-03, which matches the recorded entry date and disease. It was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 10 mg and 20 mg once daily for 6 weeks (273 enrolled; 31 on 10 mg, 121 on 20 mg, 120 on placebo) and was completed on 2022-02-25. OPC-64005 is a serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor.

The primary endpoint, change in MADRS total score at week 6 for 20 mg vs placebo, was not met. The mean changes were -10.7 on 20 mg and -9.5 on placebo, a difference of -1.1 (95% CI -3.3 to 1.0, p=0.288, MMRM). The small 10 mg arm reached -11.2 but was not formally compared with placebo. Otsuka's FY2022 consolidated results (Feb 14, 2023) state that MDD development in Japan was halted due to development strategy. The same compound's adult ADHD Phase 2 (NCT03324581) had already been discontinued. No Phase 3 trial or approval followed.

The stated reason is strategic, but the stop came straight after a clean miss on the primary endpoint at the main 20 mg dose with only a modest placebo response. That makes it a failure of the mechanism to move depression (F2). F8 is possible only as the formal wording of Otsuka's disclosure. The sources reviewed do not report target-occupancy data, so adequate engagement at 20 mg is assumed rather than shown.

It binds the serotonin (SLC6A4), norepinephrine (SLC6A2) and dopamine (SLC6A3) transporters and blocks reuptake through each, so 'decrease' is right. 2. The disease is correct. NCT04244253, 'A Phase 2 Trial of OPC-64005 for Major Depressive Disorder', started 2020-03-03, which matches the recorded entry date. MONDO:0002009 (major depressive disorder) fits. The earlier Phase 2 trial, NCT03324581 (started 2017-11-09), was in adult ADHD, a different program. 3. Several FDA-approved depression drugs act on these transporters. openFDA dates desipramine (NDA 014399) to 1964-11-20 and fluoxetine (NDA 018936) to 1987-12-29. outcome.advance_event: none; no Phase 3 trial of OPC-64005 in MDD by any sponsor (ClinicalTrials.gov lists only NCT03324581 in adult ADHD and NCT04244253 in MDD), and no FDA approval; Otsuka stopped MDD development in FY2022, inside the 4-year window
outcome.stop_reason: Otsuka's FY2022 results (Feb 14, 2023) say development for MDD in Japan 'was halted due to development strategy', after the Phase 2 trial missed its primary endpoint (MADRS week 6, 20 mg vs placebo -1.1, 95% CI -3.3 to 1.0, p=0.288)
outcome.summary:
The entry trial is NCT04244253, Otsuka's Phase 2 trial of OPC-64005 in major depressive disorder in Japan. It started on 2020-03-03, which matches the recorded entry date and disease. It was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 10 mg and 20 mg once daily for 6 weeks (273 enrolled; 31 on 10 mg, 121 on 20 mg, 120 on placebo) and was completed on 2022-02-25. OPC-64005 is a serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor.

The primary endpoint, change in MADRS total score at week 6 for 20 mg vs placebo, was not met. The mean changes were -10.7 on 20 mg and -9.5 on placebo, a difference of -1.1 (95% CI -3.3 to 1.0, p=0.288, MMRM). The small 10 mg arm reached -11.2 but was not formally compared with placebo. Otsuka's FY2022 consolidated results (Feb 14, 2023) state that MDD development in Japan was halted due to development strategy. The same compound's adult ADHD Phase 2 (NCT03324581) had already been discontinued. No Phase 3 trial or approval followed.

The stated reason is strategic, but the stop came straight after a clean miss on the primary endpoint at the main 20 mg dose with only a modest placebo response. That makes it a failure of the mechanism to move depression (F2). F8 is possible only as the formal wording of Otsuka's disclosure. The sources reviewed do not report target-occupancy data, so adequate engagement at 20 mg is assumed rather than shown.

failure_second.rationale: NCT04244253 (Otsuka, Japan, 69 sites, n=273) started on 2020-03-03 and finished primary completion on 2022-02-08. It randomized patients to OPC-64005 20 mg (n=121), 10 mg (n=31, an exploratory arm) or placebo (n=121) for 6 weeks. The primary endpoint, change from baseline in MADRS total score at week 6 for 20 mg versus placebo, was not met. The 20 mg arm improved by -10.7 and placebo by -9.5, a difference of -1.1 points (95% CI -3.3 to 1.0, MMRM p=0.288). The 10 mg arm was numerically -11.2. The results were posted on ClinicalTrials.gov on 2024-09-19. Exposure and target engagement were not the problem. The trial protocol states that overseas Phase 1 PET studies in healthy adults (277-10-205, 277-13-001, 277-14-001) confirmed brain binding to SERT, NET and DAT, and that repeated doses up to 30 mg were tolerated. Otsuka never started another MDD trial; ClinicalTrials.gov lists only this study and an earlier adult ADHD Phase 2 trial, NCT03324581, which was discontinued in August 2020. Trackers still show the MDD program at Phase 2 with no stated discontinuation, and Otsuka issued no public statement giving a reason. So a target that was engaged gave no meaningful clinical separation from placebo, which is code F2. F7 (trial design) is a weaker alternative: placebo response was large (-9.5), but the drug effect was small and its confidence interval included zero, so the trial is better read as a null result than as a failed one. The reason for stopping is inferred from the missed endpoint and the absence of any follow-on trial, not from a sponsor statement.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Pazopanib (Votrient), NDA 022465 supplement S-010, approved 2012-04-26 for advanced soft tissue sarcoma in patients who had received prior chemotherapy. Synovial sarcoma was eligible; adipocytic STS and GIST were excluded.
stop_reason: Lilly terminated CAMPFIRE JV02 (NCT04145700) after it met the protocol's futility criteria. outcome_summary:
The entry trial is NCT04145700, CAMPFIRE JV02, sponsored by Eli Lilly. It is a randomized Phase 1/2 trial in children and young adults with relapsed, recurrent or refractory synovial sarcoma, run under the CAMPFIRE master protocol (NCT05999994). It compared ramucirumab 9 mg/kg plus gemcitabine and docetaxel against gemcitabine and docetaxel alone. Its actual start date was 2020-03-04, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry, and the recorded disease (synovial sarcoma) is correct.

The trial randomized 23 participants, 16 to the ramucirumab arm and 7 to the control arm. The primary endpoint, PFS, did not differ: median PFS was 2.10 vs 2.03 months. The Bayesian posterior mean HR of 2.62 (80% CrI 1.19-4.46) points against benefit, and the success criterion was Pr(HR<1) > 99%. The objective response rate was 6.3% vs 0%. The trial was terminated because it met the protocol's futility criteria, with primary completion on 2023-02-23 and results posted in September 2023.

No Phase 3 trial and no FDA approval followed in synovial sarcoma. The drug reached the patients, which is shown by the full-dose combination regimen. VEGFR2 blockade with ramucirumab is well established in other approved indications, but it did not slow disease in this population. That makes this a case of biology not translating (F2) rather than an exposure or design failure. The sample was small, but the posterior estimate pointed toward harm, not toward a missed benefit. The sister DSRCT trial (NCT04145349) passed its futility analysis, while this one did not.

evidence.notes:
1. Ramucirumab is a human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds VEGFR2 (KDR) and blocks VEGF ligand binding, so the recorded target KDR and action 'decrease' are correct.
2. The program's Phase 2 entry trial is NCT04145700 (CAMPFIRE), a Phase 1/2 study of ramucirumab in children and young adults with synovial sarcoma. Its lead sponsor is Eli Lilly, its start date is 2020-03-04 and it was terminated. This matches the recorded disease (MONDO:0010434) and the recorded entry date.
3. Pazopanib is a multikinase inhibitor whose targets include VEGFR1, VEGFR2 (KDR) and VEGFR3, and it reduces their function. Drugs@FDA lists the soft tissue sarcoma indication as a new indication under NDA 022465 S-010, approved 2012-04-26. Pazopanib was first approved on 2009-10-19, for renal cell carcinoma.
4. The 2012 approval falls within the broad soft tissue sarcoma indication, which excluded only adipocytic sarcoma and GIST. Synovial sarcoma is a soft tissue sarcoma subtype and was enrolled in the PALETTE trial, so the approved disease is the same as or closely related to the program's disease. The approval came about 8 years before Phase 2 entry.
5. GSK held pazopanib in 2012 and Novartis holds it now. Lilly sponsors the ramucirumab program, so the precedent is not the sponsor's own drug. Lilly's own ramucirumab approval (BLA 125477, 2014-04-21, gastric cancer) is for a different disease and is not needed to support the claim.

failure_second.rationale: The decisive trial was NCT04145700 (CAMPFIRE J1S-MC-JV02), sponsored by Lilly. It was a randomized, open-label Phase 1/2 study that started on 2020-03-04 and compared ramucirumab 9 mg/kg plus gemcitabine and docetaxel against gemcitabine and docetaxel alone in children and young adults with relapsed or refractory synovial sarcoma. It enrolled 23 patients (16 ramucirumab, 7 control) and stopped on 2023-02-23. ClinicalTrials.gov gives the reason as 'Study terminated for meeting protocol specified futility criteria.' The primary endpoint, PFS, was not met. Median PFS was 2.10 months with ramucirumab and 2.03 months without it. The Bayesian posterior mean hazard ratio was 2.62 (80% CI 1.19-4.46), which points the wrong way, while success required Pr(HR<1) above 99%. ORR was 6.3% vs 0%, with no complete responses. Exposure was adequate: Cmax was 231 ug/mL, Cmin values were 73.3 and 55.4 ug/mL, and no patient developed treatment-emergent anti-drug antibodies. Those troughs are at or above the roughly 50 ug/mL linked to efficacy in adult ramucirumab studies. That adult benchmark is my own background knowledge, not something the trial record states. This rules out F1. The registry reports no safety stop, so F5 and F6 do not fit. The trial was small, but it stopped because a prespecified futility rule was met with the effect estimate pointing the wrong way, not because of enrolment or operational problems. A stronger case for F7 would need evidence the trial was cut short for operational reasons, and there is none. A target-engagement pharmacodynamic biomarker was not reported. Measured drug exposure was adequate, but adding VEGFR2 blockade did not slow disease, so this is F2 (biology did not translate). No Phase 3 trial or FDA approval for synovial sarcoma followed.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: Oncovin (vincristine sulfate, Eli Lilly), NDA 014103, approved 1963-07-10, oncology (acute leukemia); a beta-tubulin binder that inhibits polymerization. Colchicine (Colcrys, NDA 022352, 2009-07-29, gout and FMF) also binds tubulin at the colchicine site, the same site sabizabulin binds.
stop_reason: not stopped before advancing. After the Phase 3 ended, FDA did not grant an Emergency Use Authorization for COVID-19, and the registry shows no later sabizabulin ARDS trial. I did not open a source giving a formal discontinuation reason.
outcome_summary:
Entry trial: NCT04388826 is a randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 of VERU-111 (sabizabulin) in hospitalized adults with SARS-CoV-2 at high risk for ARDS. Veru Inc. (industry) sponsored it, the registry condition is 'Respiratory Distress Syndrome, Adult', and the actual start date was 2020-06-18. It completed with primary completion on 2020-12-18. Its primary endpoint was the proportion alive without respiratory failure at Day 29. The recorded entry date and disease match the registry.

What happened: Veru started Phase 3 NCT04842747 on 2021-05-18. It enrolled the same kind of patients: hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients at high risk for ARDS, with WHO ordinal score 4-6 and SpO2 at or below 94%. Its primary endpoint was death on study. The trial completed on 2022-07-06 and posted results in 2023. Sabizabulin therefore reached Phase 3 in this ARDS-risk population within 4 years. The registry condition for the Phase 3 is 'SARS-CoV Infection', but its official title and inclusion criteria target ARDS-risk patients, the same population as the Phase 2.

After that: from what I recall rather than from sources opened, the Phase 3 stopped early for efficacy with a reported reduction in mortality, and FDA did not authorize the drug for COVID-19. Sabizabulin has no approval for ARDS. The registry lists no later ARDS trial.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval of everolimus (Afinitor, NDA 022334 supplement) for progressive pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, May 2011
stop_reason: Randomized Phase 2 (I3Y-MC-JPCG) showed abemaciclib + LY3023414 was inferior to gemcitabine/capecitabine on DCR and PFS; Lilly did not pursue samotolisib further in PDAC (program later only in NCI-sponsored basket studies).
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT02981342, Lilly-sponsored randomized open-label Phase 2 of abemaciclib alone or with samotolisib (LY3023414, PI3K/mTOR) or galunisertib vs standard-of-care gemcitabine or capecitabine in previously treated metastatic PDAC, actual start 2017-01-12, completed 2018-11-09.

Results (ClinicalTrials.gov; Chiorean et al., Cancer Med 2023, PMC10652308; n=106): Stage 1 DCR 12.1% for abemaciclib + LY3023414 vs 36.4% for SOC (p=0.023); Stage 2 PFS 1.81 vs 3.25 months (log-rank p=0.0123). The authors conclude abemaciclib alone or with LY3023414 does not improve disease control or PFS vs chemotherapy. No Phase 3 followed.

Code F2: combination was dosed at its established doses with manageable safety, and CDK4/6 + PI3K/mTOR inhibition simply did not translate into benefit in unselected pretreated PDAC. Note the efficacy signal concerns the combination with abemaciclib; samotolisib was never tested as monotherapy in PDAC.

2. PDAC MONDO:0005184 is a sound mapping.

Other pre-2017 approvals on the same targets were for unrelated diseases (temsirolimus RCC 2007; everolimus RCC/breast; idelalisib PIK3CD for CLL/FL 2014). Alpelisib (PIK3CA, 2019) postdates entry.

Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT03446846 is Minerva Neurosciences' randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2b of MIN-117 at 5.0 mg and 2.5 mg in adults with moderate to severe MDD with anxious distress. Actual start was 2018-03-30, n=360, and it is the only industry Phase 2 for MDD on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Outcome: on 2019-12-18 Minerva reported that neither dose separated from placebo on the 6-week change in MADRS (primary) or HAM-A (key secondary). The only nominal signal was a 1.6-point HAM-A improvement at week 2 on 2.5 mg. Posted results show identical MADRS changes of about -12 in all three arms. The drug was generally well tolerated, with AE incidence comparable to placebo. Minerva then stopped development (Fierce Biotech; Benzinga).

claim: Human germline genetics established, before the program entered Phase 2, a mechanism for this target in this disease that the drug's action opposes (e.g. risk variants raise the gene's function and the drug lowers it, or loss-of-function variants are protective and the drug lowers function, or loss-of-function causes the disease and the drug raises function).
evidence_source: Bell DW et al. 'Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR.' Nat Genet 2005;37:1315-1316 (PMID 16258541), which describes a family with germline EGFR T790M and lung adenocarcinoma.
stop_reason: n/a; approved in China (NMPA) for EGFR-mutant NSCLC but not approved by FDA
outcome_summary:
ASK120067 is limertinib, a third-generation EGFR TKI from Jiangsu Aosaikang (ASK Pharm), partnered with Innovent. Its first industry trial with a Phase 2 component, NCT03502850 (Phase 1/2 in locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with EGFR T790M), started 2017-11-30. That matches the pipeline date.

The Phase 3 NCT04143607 (limertinib vs gefitinib first-line in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, primary endpoint PFS; 337 patients) started 2019-07-23, well within 4 years. It met its primary endpoint: median PFS 20.7 vs 9.7 months, a 56% risk reduction, with CNS PFS 20.7 vs 7.1 months.

outcome_summary:
The earliest industry trial of cipaglucosidase alfa (ATB200, given with the stabilizer AT2221/miglustat) in Pompe disease (GSD II) is NCT02675465 (ATB200-02, Amicus). It is a combined Phase 1/2 first-in-human study whose primary endpoints are safety and PK, and it started in April 2016, matching the pipeline date. The entry is 'partial' because the trial is Phase 1/2.

The program advanced within 4 years. The Phase 3 PROPEL trial (NCT03729362) compared cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat with alglucosidase alfa plus placebo in late-onset Pompe disease and actually started on 2018-12-04. Further Phase 3 trials followed (NCT04138277, NCT03911505, NCT04808505). The FDA approved Pombiliti (cipaglucosidase alfa-atga) with Opfolda (miglustat) on 2023-09-28 for adults with late-onset Pompe disease who weigh at least 40 kg and are not improving on their current ERT. The EMA approved it in 2023.

PROPEL's primary endpoint, 6MWD change at week 52, did not reach statistical superiority over alglucosidase alfa under the prespecified analysis. The posted results include an MMRM p-value of 0.048, but Amicus and the Lancet Neurology 2021 paper report superiority as not met. FVC favored cipaglucosidase alfa. Since PROPEL still led to approval, the program is coded not_a_failure.

outcome_summary:
Earliest industry Phase 2 in NSCLC is NCT02834936 (Jiangsu Hengrui; single-arm pyrotinib in advanced HER2-mutant NSCLC, n=60), actual start 2016-10-20, matching the pipeline date. (An earlier investigator-sponsored Phase 2, NCT02535507 by Tongji University, 2015, is not industry-sponsored.)

Hengrui started the randomized Phase 3 PYRAMID-1 (NCT04447118; pyrotinib vs docetaxel after platinum, HER2 exon 20 mutation, n=151) on 2020-09-11 (actual), about 5-6 weeks inside the 4-year window, so the program advanced. ClinicalTrials.gov lists it as completed with primary completion 2023-06-02 and no posted results; I found no published primary PFS result and no NMPA/FDA approval of pyrotinib for NSCLC (pyrotinib is approved in China only for HER2+ breast cancer). Status is therefore active/unclear with primary endpoint not reported.

evidence.earliest_source: Bell DW et al., 'Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR', Nat Genet 2005 (PMID 16258541)
evidence.notes:
1. Pyrotinib is an irreversible pan-HER TKI (EGFR/HER1, HER2, HER4). Targets EGFR+ERBB2 and the 'decreases' action are correct; HER4 (ERBB4) is omitted but is a minor target.
2. MONDO:0005233 NSCLC correctly maps the indication (the trial was in HER2-mutant advanced NSCLC).

Bell 2005 described one family carrying germline EGFR T790M (an activating, gain-of-function allele) with multiple NSCLC cases. Gain-of-function risk alleles fit a drug that lowers EGFR/HER2 activity.

ClinVar classifies EGFR T790M only as 'drug response' and ERBB2 G660D as 'uncertain significance', and no GWAS lead for NSCLC maps to EGFR or ERBB2 coding function. The main EGFR/ERBB2 NSCLC mechanism is somatic. Also, the pyrotinib trial targets somatic HER2 mutations, not germline carriers. So 'established' overstates it, and the claim is partial.
5. The authors are academic (MGH/Dana-Farber, Japanese academic groups), not Jiangsu Hengrui.

outcome_summary:
Mavelertinib (PF-06747775) is Pfizer's irreversible mutant-selective EGFR (Del19/L858R ± T790M) inhibitor. Its only industry trial in NSCLC is the Phase 1/2 study NCT02349633, actual start 2015-05-14, matching the pipeline date. The study included monotherapy dose escalation, combinations with palbociclib and avelumab, and a Phase 2 cohort 2B (PF-06747775 ± palbociclib).

Pfizer stopped development and terminated the study for strategic reasons tied to the changing external environment. CT.gov notes the safety profile and benefit-risk were unchanged, and secondary sources tie the stop to osimertinib's first-line approval. Results on CT.gov show few DLTs in escalation. In the 200 mg QD group there were 11 confirmed partial responses and no complete responses. The Phase 2 PFS comparison was not completed as planned. The phase 1b/2 publication (Expert Opin Investig Drugs 2022) describes the early termination. No Phase 3 was started.

This was a portfolio/commercial decision (F8). The truncated Phase 2 efficacy endpoint was not formally evaluated, so the primary endpoint is recorded as not reported.

evidence.earliest_source: Bell DW et al., 'Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR', Nat Genet 2005;37:1315-1316 (PMID 16258541); extended by Oxnard GR et al., J Thorac Oncol 2012 (PMID 22588155)
evidence.notes:
1. Mavelertinib (PF-06747775, Pfizer) is a covalent, mutant-selective third-generation EGFR TKI (Del19/L858R +/- T790M); target EGFR and inhibitory action correct.
2. MONDO:0005233 non-small cell lung carcinoma is appropriate; trial NCT02349633 (Phase 1/2, start 2015-05-14) enrolls EGFR-mutant NSCLC, matching the recorded entry date.

The germline evidence is limited: Bell 2005 described a family with inherited EGFR T790M (an activating/gain-of-function variant) segregating with NSCLC, and Oxnard 2012 estimated germline T790M in ~1% of NSCLC with T790M and an elevated lung cancer risk in carriers. This is a gain-of-function germline risk variant opposed by an EGFR inhibitor (and T790M is precisely what mavelertinib targets), so the direction fits, but it rests on rare familial/case-series data with no GWAS or population-scale support, hence partial.
4. Neither source is authored by Pfizer.
5. No data error found.

evidence_source: Romeo S et al., 'Rare loss-of-function mutations in ANGPTL family members contribute to plasma triglyceride levels in humans', J Clin Invest 2009;119:70-79 (PMID 19075393). Confirmed by Musunuru K et al., NEJM 2010 (PMID 20942659): ANGPTL3 LoF causes familial combined hypolipidemia.
stop_reason: Pfizer and Ionis announced discontinuation on 2022-01-31: the magnitude of non-HDL-C and triglyceride lowering did not support development for CV risk reduction or severe hypertriglyceridemia, and vupanorsen caused dose-dependent increases in hepatic fat with ALT/AST elevations at higher doses. Rights returned to Ionis.
outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry confirmed: NCT04516291 (TRANSLATE-TIMI 70), Pfizer-sponsored dose-ranging Phase 2b of vupanorsen (AKCEA-ANGPTL3-LRx) in dyslipidemia/hyperlipidemia on statins, actual start 2020-09-28, completed 2021-12-06. Earlier Ionis/Akcea Phase 2s (2017-2018) targeted FCS, hypertriglyceridemia with T2D/NAFLD and FPL rather than hyperlipidemia per se, so 2020-09-28 is the earliest industry Phase 2 for this disease framing.

Primary endpoint met: non-HDL-C percent change at week 24 ranged -22% to -28% vs -1.1% placebo (all p<0.001, posted results; Bergmark et al., Circulation 2022). LDL-C reductions were modest, and dose-dependent hepatic fat increases with ALT/AST elevations at higher doses were seen. Pfizer/Ionis discontinued the program on 2022-01-31.

Code F6, with an F2 element: the liver-fat/transaminase signal is attributed to the antisense molecule (not seen with ANGPTL3 antibody evinacumab), and it capped dosing at efficacy that was commercially insufficient. One could argue F2/F8 because the stop also cited inadequate lipid-lowering magnitude despite near-complete ANGPTL3 knockdown.

evidence.earliest_source: Romeo S et al., 'Rare loss-of-function mutations in ANGPTL family members contribute to plasma triglyceride levels in humans', J Clin Invest 2009;119:70-79 (PMID 19075393). Confirmed by Musunuru K et al., NEJM 2010 (PMID 20942659): ANGPTL3 LoF causes familial combined hypolipidemia.
evidence.notes:
1. Vupanorsen (AKCEA-ANGPTL3-LRx / ISIS 703802 / PF-07285557) is a GalNAc-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide that lowers hepatic ANGPTL3 mRNA; target ANGPTL3, action 'decreases', correct.
2. Hyperlipidemia (MONDO:0021187) fits the Phase 2 population (TRANSLATE-TIMI 70, NCT04516291: elevated non-HDL-C and triglycerides).
3. Human germline LoF in ANGPTL3 lowers TG (Romeo 2009, Dallas Heart Study resequencing). Biallelic LoF causes familial combined hypolipidemia with low LDL-C, HDL-C and TG (Musunuru 2010). GWAS identified the ANGPTL3 locus for TG/LDL (Kathiresan 2009 Nat Genet, PMID 19060906). Heterozygous LoF carriers have lower lipids and less CAD (Stitziel 2017 JACC, PMID 28385496; Dewey 2017 NEJM, PMID 28538136). LoF is protective and the drug lowers function, so the drug's action matches the protective direction.
4. All of these predate 2020-09-28. Romeo 2009 and Musunuru 2010 (UT Southwestern/Broad/Penn academic groups) are not sponsor-authored. Graham 2017 NEJM (PMID 28538111) did involve Ionis and is the sponsor's own paper, but it is not the earliest.

OCTA12 is a recombinant human von Willebrand factor fragment dimer. Octapharma combined it with OCTA8 (human-cl rhFVIII, the Nuwiq intermediate) to make OCTA101, a subcutaneous FVIII product. The drug was not stopped for lack of exposure or efficacy. It was stopped because the subcutaneous rFVIII/VWF-fragment product provoked an immune response, which is molecule- and route-specific toxicity (F6). One could argue F5, since the immune response targets FVIII itself, but the trigger is the product and its route rather than the intended mechanism.

claim: Human germline genetics established, before the program entered Phase 2, a mechanism for this target in this disease that the drug's action opposes (e.g. risk variants raise the gene's function and the drug lowers it, or loss-of-function variants are protective and the drug lowers function, or loss-of-function causes the disease and the drug raises function).
evidence_source: Bell DW et al., "Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR", Nat Genet 2005;37(12):1315-6 (PMID 16258541, Massachusetts General Hospital). It reports a family with several cases of NSCLC and germline transmission of EGFR T790M. Vikis H et al., Cancer Res 2007 (PMID 17510392), showed that germline T790M is an allele with enhanced kinase activity that gives cells a growth advantage.
outcome_summary:
Aumolertinib (HS-10296/almonertinib; Hansoh) entered industry-sponsored Phase 2 in NSCLC through the Phase 1/2 APOLLO trial NCT02981108, which started 2017-05-08. That trial's Phase 2 part had ORR as its primary endpoint and enrolled 244 T790M+ patients. Within 4 years the program reached Phase 3: AENEAS (NCT03849768) started 2019-02-01. It met its primary endpoint of investigator-assessed PFS versus gefitinib: 19.3 vs 9.9 months, HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.36-0.60, P<.0001 (JCO 2022, PMID 35580297). China's NMPA approved Ameile on 2020-03-17 for T790M+ NSCLC after prior EGFR-TKI therapy, and the drug remains marketed in China. Many further Phase 3 trials are listed, including adjuvant, post-chemoradiation and combination studies.

Outside China the path was rockier, but these setbacks were regulatory or partner decisions, not efficacy or safety findings. EQRx licensed ex-China rights in July 2020. In November 2022 it said the FDA would not accept an interim monotherapy comparison and pushed a US filing to 2027, contingent on a Phase 3b against osimertinib (NCT05493501). EQRx terminated that trial and gave notice on 2023-08-01 that it was ending the license as part of a pipeline wind-down tied to its merger with Revolution Medicines. The CT.gov record says the trial was stopped for corporate reasons, "not related to any efficacy or safety issues."

The EU granted approval (Aumseqa) on 2026-02-12 for first-line EGFR ex19del/L858R and for T790M+ NSCLC, according to Hansoh's press release. Secondary reports say the European Commission revoked that authorisation on 2026-09-25 on a procedural, data-exclusivity issue (referencing osimertinib data) and that Hansoh resubmitted in late September 2026; this was not checked against a primary EC/EMA document.

The FDA has not approved the drug. Overall the program advanced and is approved for this disease in China, so this is not a failure.

The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of pabinafusp alfa (JR-141) in MPS II is NCT03128593, a Phase 1/2 study in 14 Japanese patients sponsored by JCR Pharmaceuticals. ClinicalTrials.gov records its actual start as 2017-03-30, matching the pipeline date. A Brazilian Phase 2 trial (NCT03359213) followed in July 2018.

JCR started the Japanese Phase 2/3 study NCT03568175 on 2018-08-01. It was single-arm, enrolled 28 patients and was completed 2020-02-20. Its primary endpoint was change in cerebrospinal-fluid heparan sulfate, which fell significantly, as published by Okuyama et al. in Mol Ther 2021. On that basis Japan approved the drug as IZCARGO in 2021. A Phase 2/3 start counts as a Phase 3 start, so the program advanced within 4 years. The caveat is that the global randomized Phase 3 STARLIGHT (NCT04573023) started 2022-02-14, about 4.9 years after entry, and that there is no FDA approval.

Now: pabinafusp alfa is marketed in Japan. STARLIGHT is active, not recruiting; JCR announced in July 2025 that enrollment was complete. On 2026-10-02 JCR and Italfarmaco signed an exclusive license for the US, Europe and Latin America, aimed at FDA, EMA, MHRA and ANVISA approvals.

evidence.notes:
1. Pabinafusp alfa (JR-141; JCR Pharmaceuticals) is an anti-human transferrin receptor antibody fused to iduronate-2-sulfatase. It is enzyme replacement that crosses the blood-brain barrier, so target IDS and 'increases target function' are correct.

The enzyme deficiency was shown in 1973 (Bach et al.); Wilson et al. 1990 cloned IDS and found gene alterations in patient DNA, and many point mutations were reported in the early 1990s. 4. All sources predate the 2017 Phase 2 entry by decades. They are academic, not JCR. No data errors found; the 2017-03-30 date is consistent with the Japanese Phase 1/2 start.

outcome_summary:
The earliest industry Phase 2 trial of tividenofusp alfa (DNL310, Denali) in MPS II is NCT04251026, a Phase 1/2 open-label study in pediatric Hunter syndrome with actual start 2020-07-16, matching the pipeline date.

evidence.earliest_source: Geisterfer-Lowrance AA, Kass S, Tanigawa G, Vosberg HP, McKenna W, Seidman CE, Seidman JG. 'A molecular basis for familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a beta cardiac myosin heavy chain gene missense mutation.' Cell 1990;62(5):999-1006, PMID 1975517. It reports the germline MYH7 R403Q missense variant (ClinVar VCV000014087 / RCV000015143) segregating with familial HCM.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. Green et al., Science 2016 (PMID 26912705, published Feb 2016, before Phase 2 entry) says MYK-461 'reduces contractility by decreasing the ATPase activity of the cardiac myosin heavy chain'. The FDA Camzyos label (2022) calls mavacamten 'an allosteric and reversible inhibitor selective for cardiac myosin'. It acts on cardiac myosin generally: the mouse efficacy work used alpha-MHC (Myh6) mutants. MYH7 (beta-cardiac MHC) is still the correct human ventricular target.

(2) The disease matches. NCT02842242 (PIONEER-HCM, MyoKardia, Phase 2, actual start 2016-08) enrolled symptomatic obstructive HCM patients (conditions 'Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic Obstructive'; LV wall >=15 mm; LVOT gradient >=30 mmHg at rest). That is a subset of HCM (MONDO:0005045).

(3) The claim is only partly supported. Germline genetics clearly showed before 2016 that dominant MYH7 missense variants cause HCM (Geisterfer-Lowrance 1990, Cell). The direction (gain of function, which an inhibitor opposes) did not come from germline genetics. It came from in-vitro and mouse functional studies, and those disagreed before entry:
- Showed enhanced function: Tyska 2000 Circ Res (PMID 10764406; mouse R403Q had 2.3x ATPase, 2.2x force and 1.6x sliding velocity); Palmiter 2000 (PMID 11227787; 'enhanced mechanical performance'); Sommese 2013 PNAS (PMID 23798412; human R453C had +50% intrinsic force but -30% ATPase and velocity).
- Showed reduced function: Cuda 1993 JCI (PMID 8514894; mutant beta-myosin moved actin slower); Nag 2015 Sci Adv (PMID 26601291), which calls R403Q 'the most debated HCM-causing mutation' with 'no consensus' on its mechanism and found a loss of contractility in human beta-cardiac R403Q.
- Spudich 2015 (PMID 25619247) offered increased power output only as a 'possible unifying hypothesis'.
- Green 2016 itself concedes that 'some in vitro studies ... are consistent with mutant sarcomeres exhibiting enhanced contractile power, others are not', and leans on the hyperdynamic clinical phenotype.
- The super-relaxed-state work cited in our mechanism label came after entry.

So causality predates entry, but the opposed-direction mechanism was a contested hypothesis in Aug 2016.

(4) Our database dates for the ClinVar rows are wrong:
- RCV000015143 (R403Q) is dated 1961. That year comes from Pare et al. 1961, Am J Med (PMID 13732753), a clinical description of the kindred, not genetic evidence. The variant-level evidence dates to 1990.
- RCV000015182 (MYH7 L1793P, an OMIM assertion with no assertion criteria) is dated 1971. That is Cancilla 1971, Neurology (PMID 4104682), a skeletal myopathy kindred. The variant was found in 2006 (Dye et al., PMID 16684601) in myosin storage myopathy. Its link to HCM is weak, and it is not good HCM evidence.

(5) Sponsor authorship: the 1990 paper came from the Seidman lab at Brigham and Women's / Harvard, 22 years before MyoKardia existed. The S-1 says MyoKardia was incorporated in June 2012 by Third Rock Ventures. However, C.E. Seidman and J.G. Seidman, and also J.A. Spudich and L.A. Leinwand (authors of the 2013–2015 functional papers), are disclosed as MyoKardia founders and shareholders in Green 2016. So the key paper is not sponsor-authored, but its authors later co-founded the sponsor.
